column5:
A successful first Global Dialogue would establish three foundations.

First, shared recognition of the catastrophic and existential risks posed by the race to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI). Frontier AI labs publicly state that they are racing to build systems more capable than humans across virtually all cognitive tasks, with timelines they themselves estimate in years rather than decades. The CEOs of the leading AI companies, alongside hundreds of the field's most cited scientists, have signed statements declaring that "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." A Dialogue that does not begin from this shared recognition will not be addressing the most consequential governance question of our time.

Second, an explicit acknowledgement that existing governance efforts are insufficient. Voluntary commitments from frontier developers have repeatedly been broken. National regulations focus primarily on deployment risks rather than the development of increasingly capable frontier systems. The Dialogue should map these gaps honestly and commit to closing them.

Third, a concrete pathway toward binding international coordination on frontier AI development. This is the unique value the UN can provide. Just as the international community developed treaties for nuclear weapons, biological weapons, and ozone-depleting substances, frontier AI requires binding multilateral instruments. A successful first Dialogue would establish a working track toward such an instrument, including: (a) shared definitions of frontier capabilities warranting international oversight, (b) verification and compliance mechanisms drawing on precedents like the IAEA, and (c) a clear timeline for negotiation.

Success is not consensus on every issue. Success is the Dialogue establishing itself as the venue where the hardest question, namely how humanity collectively governs the development of systems that may match or exceed human capabilities, is genuinely on the table.
column6: Safe, secure and trustworthy AI;Interoperability of governance approaches;Transparency, accountability, and human oversight;Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;
column7:
Safe, secure and trustworthy AI is our highest priority because the central governance challenge of our time is the uncontrolled race to develop artificial general intelligence. Frontier developers themselves acknowledge that the alignment problem, namely ensuring advanced AI systems pursue intended goals without catastrophic side effects, is unsolved. Deploying systems whose behaviour we cannot reliably predict or control, at capability levels approaching or exceeding human performance, represents an unprecedented risk to international peace and security. The UN must address this directly.

Interoperability of governance approaches matters because frontier AI development is a coordination problem. Unilateral national restrictions are undermined by jurisdictional arbitrage. Without binding international coordination on the most capable systems, every government faces pressure to deregulate to avoid losing the race. Only a multilateral framework can break this dynamic. The Dialogue is uniquely positioned to lay the groundwork for such a framework, drawing on precedents from arms control, biosafety and environmental treaties.

Transparency, accountability, and human oversight are foundational. Frontier AI systems are currently developed behind closed doors, with limited external scrutiny of their capabilities, training processes, or safety evaluations. Governments and the public lack the information needed to make informed decisions about acceptable risk. International requirements for capability disclosure, third-party auditing, incident reporting, and meaningful human control over consequential decisions are essential preconditions for any other governance effort to succeed.

Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI is critical because the economic disruption already underway, particularly the rapid automation of cognitive labour, threatens to concentrate wealth and power, destabilise democracies, and erode the social fabric that any governance regime depends on. Addressing AGI risks requires also addressing the economic transformation happening now, which is rapidly reshaping the political conditions under which governance decisions will be made.
column8:
Three cross-cutting issues warrant explicit attention.

First, the development of frontier AI systems as a category distinct from AI deployment. Most existing governance frameworks focus on how AI is used. The greater risks come from what is being built: increasingly general, increasingly autonomous systems whose capabilities are not fully understood even by their developers. The Dialogue must distinguish frontier development from narrow application, and recognise that the former requires its own governance regime, including thresholds above which international oversight becomes mandatory.

Second, the option of pausing or restricting the development of frontier AI systems beyond defined capability thresholds. Current discourse treats continued capability scaling as inevitable. It is not. The international community has repeatedly chosen to restrict or prohibit technologies whose risks outweighed their benefits, including biological weapons, human cloning, and certain classes of autonomous weapons. A Global Dialogue that does not include the option of binding restrictions on frontier development is foreclosing the most direct response to the most serious risk. We urge the Dialogue to treat a coordinated international pause on frontier AI development beyond agreed capability thresholds as a credible policy option, not a fringe position.

Third, democratic legitimacy and meaningful public participation. Decisions about AI development are currently being made by a small number of private actors and the governments closest to them. The trajectory of a technology that may reshape every aspect of human life cannot legitimately be set by this narrow group. The Dialogue should commit to mechanisms that bring affected communities, workers, civil society, and the global public into substantive decision-making, not merely consultative roles. Citizens' assemblies, structured public deliberation, and binding civil society representation in governance bodies are concrete tools the UN should champion.

These three issues, namely frontier development as a distinct category, pause as a credible option, and democratic legitimacy, cut across all four thematic clusters.
column9:
PauseAI is a global federation of civil society organisations operating in over 15 countries, representing citizens concerned about catastrophic and existential risks from frontier AI development. Here is how the governance gaps in the thematic areas we selected affect us.

On safety and trustworthiness: Frontier AI labs are now using their own models to accelerate development of the next generation, with credible reports of recursive self-improvement loops shortening already short timelines. Our members include researchers, parents, students and workers who recognise that no government has the visibility, let alone the authority, to determine whether the next generation of frontier systems can be developed safely. This is not a future concern. Models being trained today will be deployed within 6-12 months under governance frameworks designed for a previous generation of technology.

On interoperability: Our chapters in the EU, UK, Canada, Kenya, Germany, France, Czech Republic and elsewhere observe firsthand how jurisdictional fragmentation undermines national efforts. Developers headquartered in lightly regulated jurisdictions release systems that affect citizens everywhere. National governments tell our advocates privately that they cannot act alone without disadvantaging their domestic industries. This coordination failure is the central obstacle to meaningful governance, and it can only be resolved multilaterally.

On transparency and oversight: Our volunteers, including AI researchers and former employees of frontier labs, repeatedly encounter the same problem: the information needed to assess risk is held privately by developers, with limited disclosure to even the most capable national regulators. Civil society and the public are excluded entirely.

On economic and social implications: Our chapters are increasingly engaged with unions, student organisations and worker associations whose constituencies are experiencing rapid AI-driven displacement. The opportunity is significant. These communities are mobilising and seek a constructive governance pathway. The risk is that without one, public concern consolidates into reactive backlash rather than informed participation.
column10:
The AI Dialogue can play a role no other forum currently fills: serving as the universal, legitimate venue where binding international coordination on frontier AI development is genuinely on the table.

Establishing shared facts. Existing forums often operate from divergent assumptions about AI capabilities, timelines and risks. The Dialogue can convene authoritative scientific assessments, drawing on the model of the IPCC, that establish a shared evidence base on frontier AI capabilities, risks and governance options. The International AI Safety Report led by Yoshua Bengio is a useful starting point that the UN should institutionalise and expand.

Legitimising the full range of policy options. Current international discourse treats continued frontier capability scaling as inevitable. The Dialogue can change this by treating the full range of governance options as legitimate subjects of negotiation, including capability thresholds above which development requires international authorisation, compute governance, and coordinated pauses on specific classes of development. The UN's unique convening authority makes it the only body that can credibly place these options on the global agenda.

Building toward binding instruments. Voluntary commitments from frontier developers have repeatedly proven insufficient. The Dialogue should establish a clear pathway from deliberation toward binding multilateral instruments, drawing on precedents including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Biological Weapons Convention, and the Montreal Protocol. Each of these emerged from sustained international dialogue that produced real obligations, verification mechanisms and institutional capacity.

Ensuring universal participation. Frontier AI is currently being developed in a small number of jurisdictions, with consequences for every country on Earth. The Dialogue is the only forum where every state, regardless of its current AI capacity, has standing to participate in shaping the rules. This legitimacy is not symbolic. It is the precondition for any governance regime that will hold over time.
column11:
The Dialogue should connect with several existing initiatives while providing distinctive added value.

Scientific assessment infrastructure. The International AI Safety Report, produced by an independent expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio with contributions from 30+ countries, provides a strong foundation for shared scientific understanding. The Dialogue should institutionalise this report under UN auspices, giving it the authority and continuity needed to inform negotiations.

National and regional governance frameworks. The EU AI Act, the UK and US AI Safety Institutes, the Bletchley and Seoul Declarations, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI represent the most developed governance work to date. The Dialogue should map these frameworks for compatibility and gaps, identifying where international harmonisation is achievable and where the absence of binding multilateral instruments leaves critical risks ungoverned.

The AI Safety Institute network. The emerging network of national AI Safety Institutes provides important technical capacity for evaluation and red-teaming. The Dialogue should support its expansion to all interested member states and connect it to the UN system, ensuring evaluation capacity is not concentrated in a handful of jurisdictions.

Civil society and affected communities. Networks including PauseAI, the Future of Life Institute, the Centre for AI Safety, professional bodies, labour organisations, and academic communities represent constituencies directly engaged with AI risks. The Dialogue should establish formal mechanisms for substantive civil society participation.

The Dialogue's distinctive added value is universal legitimacy, the authority to address frontier development as a distinct governance category, and the mandate to move from voluntary coordination toward binding multilateral instruments. No other body combines these three.
column12:
The Dialogue should distinguish between consultative participation and substantive participation, and ensure both are meaningful.

Member states should hold decision-making authority, consistent with the UN's intergovernmental character.

Frontier AI developers should participate, but with clear acknowledgement that they have direct commercial interests in the outcome. Their input should be transparent, on the record, and balanced by equivalent representation from independent scientific and civil society voices. The model of industry self-governance has been tried and has produced insufficient results.

Whistleblowers and former employees of frontier AI developers require dedicated channels and protections. A growing number of researchers and engineers who have worked at the frontier of AI development have left their organisations citing serious safety concerns. Their firsthand knowledge of internal practices, safety cultures and capabilities is uniquely valuable and unavailable through any other source. The Dialogue should establish formal mechanisms for their testimony, with appropriate legal protections against retaliation, non-disparagement clauses and other instruments currently used to silence them.

Independent technical experts, particularly those without financial ties to frontier developers, should have standing equivalent to industry representatives. The International AI Safety Report panel offers a useful template.

Civil society, including organisations representing workers, students, affected communities and citizens concerned about catastrophic risks, requires formal mechanisms for substantive input, not only consultative roles.

The structure should include both plenary deliberation and thematic working groups producing concrete deliverables on a defined timeline.
column13:
Several constituencies are systematically underrepresented in current AI governance discussions.

Affected workers and communities. The people whose livelihoods, public services and information environments are being reshaped by AI deployment are largely absent from the rooms where governance decisions are made. Trade unions, professional associations, teachers, healthcare workers, creative workers and others experiencing AI-driven changes firsthand have direct knowledge that current discussions lack. The Dialogue should establish formal mechanisms for their participation.

Citizens concerned about catastrophic and existential risks. A significant and growing share of the global public, reflected in polling across multiple countries, expresses serious concern about the trajectory of frontier AI development. This constituency is currently represented almost exclusively by a small number of expert organisations and is largely absent from intergovernmental forums. The Dialogue should treat public concern about catastrophic risks as a legitimate input to governance, not a fringe view to be managed.

Future generations. AI governance decisions made now will shape the conditions under which all subsequent generations live. No current institutional mechanism represents their interests. The Dialogue should consider formal mechanisms for representing future generations, drawing on precedents including Wales's Future Generations Commissioner and the UN Secretary-General's proposed Envoy for Future Generations.

Independent scientific voices. Researchers without commercial ties to frontier developers, particularly those raising concerns about catastrophic risks, are often outweighed in current forums by industry-affiliated experts. The Dialogue should correct this imbalance.
column14: Honest assessment: This question is not central to PauseAI's mission, and we have no distinctive expertise on UN process design.
column15:
Several existing policies and approaches offer useful foundations, though we note honestly that none yet adequately addresses frontier AI development.

Capability thresholds and compute governance. The EU AI Act's designation of "general-purpose AI models with systemic risk" above defined compute thresholds, and similar provisions in the US Executive Order 14110 (since rescinded), establish the principle that frontier systems warrant different treatment based on capability. This principle is sound; the thresholds, enforcement mechanisms and international coordination remain inadequate.

Pre-deployment evaluation and red-teaming. The UK and US AI Safety Institutes' work evaluating frontier models before deployment, including the agreements with leading developers to test models pre-release, establishes important precedent. This capacity should be expanded internationally and made mandatory rather than voluntary.

Whistleblower protections. California SB 53 (Artificial intelligence models: large developers, 2025) establishes whistleblower protections specifically for frontier AI employees. This is the first law of its kind globally and offers a template for international adoption.

Treaty precedents for binding restrictions. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Biological Weapons Convention, the Chemical Weapons Convention, and the Montreal Protocol all demonstrate that the international community can negotiate binding restrictions on dangerous technologies, with verification mechanisms, when the stakes warrant it. The IAEA's verification regime for nuclear materials offers a particularly relevant institutional model for compute governance.

Citizens' assemblies on technology governance. France's Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat and Ireland's citizens' assemblies demonstrate that structured public deliberation can produce considered judgement on complex governance trade-offs.

What is currently missing. No existing initiative establishes binding international restrictions on the development of frontier AI systems beyond defined capability thresholds. This is the central governance gap. The Dialogue's most important contribution would be to begin closing it.

column5: A successful first Global Dialogue on AI Governance would produce outcomes that are genuinely inclusive of voices from the Global South - particularly Africa, where AI adoption is accelerating but governance frameworks remain nascent. Success would mean: first, the adoption of clear recommendations that acknowledge the digital infrastructure divide, recognizing that meaningful AI governance must address connectivity gaps, energy access limitations, and the lack of localized datasets that currently hinder AI deployment across African communities. Second, the Dialogue should yield actionable commitments to bridge the AI capacity gap - investing in technical education, digital skills, and local AI development ecosystems that empower nations to build, not just consume, AI tools. Third, success requires centering ethical AI principles that reflect diverse cultural, linguistic, and social contexts - not frameworks designed solely for high-income economies. This includes commitments to address gender bias in AI systems, ensuring women and girls are not further marginalized by algorithmic decision-making in health, finance, education, and employment. Fourth, the Dialogue should produce a roadmap for inclusive AI governance architecture that brings civil society, private sector innovators, academia, and marginalized communities into formal governance spaces - not just as observers but as co-creators of standards. Finally, a concrete follow-up mechanism to track implementation, with representation from underrepresented regions, would signal that this Dialogue is more than symbolic - it is the foundation of an equitable AI future.
column6: Safe, secure and trustworthy AI;AI capacity-building;Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;Protection and promotion of human rights;
column7: These four themes are interconnected and critical from an African civil society perspective. Safe, secure and trustworthy AI is foundational - without trust, AI adoption will stall or cause harm, particularly in communities with limited recourse mechanisms. AI capacity-building is urgent for Africa: the continent cannot meaningfully participate in AI governance if it lacks the human capital and infrastructure to develop, deploy, and evaluate AI systems locally. Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI captures the breadth of challenges we face on the ground - from AI models trained on non-African data producing biased outputs, to cultural erasure through homogenized language models, to economic disruption in informal labor markets. Critically, gender bias in AI systems disproportionately affects women and girls in Africa, reinforcing existing inequalities in hiring tools, credit scoring, and health diagnostics. Finally, protection and promotion of human rights ensures that AI governance is anchored in dignity and non-discrimination - essential where regulatory oversight is nascent and communities are most vulnerable to algorithmic harm. Together, these themes reflect the governance priorities of the 1.4 billion people on the African continent who are both AI's greatest potential beneficiaries and its most underprotected.
column8: Several critical cross-cutting issues remain underrepresented in the current thematic framework. First, AI infrastructure inequality deserves explicit attention. In many African nations, unstable power supply, limited broadband connectivity, and the absence of local data centers make AI deployment not just difficult but inequitable. Governance frameworks that do not address physical and digital infrastructure gaps will remain disconnected from lived realities. Second, gender-responsive AI governance is a cross-cutting gap. Gender bias is not merely an ethical issue - it is an infrastructure, economic, and rights issue simultaneously. AI systems deployed in agriculture, health, and finance in Africa frequently underperform for women due to biased training data and male-dominated design processes. A standalone thematic commitment to gender-responsive AI is warranted. Third, the local context adaptation of AI models needs formal governance attention. Global AI systems often fail to account for indigenous languages, local legal contexts, and culturally specific norms. AI governance must include mechanisms to validate and adapt AI models for local deployment rather than assuming global models are universally appropriate. Fourth, youth and intergenerational equity in AI is an emerging issue: young people in Africa are among the most exposed to AI-driven labor disruption and the least represented in governance processes. Deliberate inclusion of youth voices in formal AI governance structures is essential for long-term legitimacy and relevance.
column9: In Nigeria and across Sub-Saharan Africa, governance gaps in AI are producing compounding challenges with significant real-world consequences. The most immediate challenge is the absence of a localized AI regulatory framework. While Nigeria has introduced a National AI Policy, implementation remains nascent, leaving a vacuum where commercial AI systems operate without meaningful oversight. This gap is acutely felt in sectors like financial technology, healthcare, and agriculture, where AI tools are being rapidly deployed but without mechanisms for accountability or redress when they fail. Infrastructure gaps compound this governance deficit. Unreliable electricity, limited broadband penetration outside urban centers, and prohibitively expensive data costs mean that many communities are subject to AI decisions - in credit scoring, recruitment screening, or government service delivery - without the ability to access, question, or challenge those systems. From a civil society and gender perspective, AI systems trained predominantly on Western, male-skewed datasets routinely misidentify, misclassify, or exclude African women. In the work of PAWA Initiative and Shecode.ai, we observe this in how women-led small businesses are disadvantaged by AI-driven credit risk models and how female professionals are underrepresented in AI-generated content or recommendations. On the opportunity side, Africa's youthful population and rapidly expanding digital economy position the continent as a major beneficiary of well-governed AI. Investments in local AI talent pipelines, open and representative datasets, and inclusive policy design processes could accelerate development outcomes significantly. The AI Dialogue offers a critical moment to ensure governance frameworks create enabling conditions - not barriers - for Africa's AI future.
column10: The AI Dialogue has a unique opportunity to serve as the primary multilateral platform for building consensus on AI governance principles that are binding, inclusive, and enforceable - not merely aspirational. Its most critical role in international cooperation is ensuring that AI governance does not replicate existing global power imbalances, where technology standards are set by a handful of high-income nations and adopted by the rest as non-negotiable defaults. The Dialogue can advance cooperation by establishing a South-South and North-South knowledge exchange architecture on AI governance - enabling countries like Nigeria, Kenya, Rwanda, and Ghana, which are building domestic AI frameworks, to share experiences and receive targeted support. It should also promote common interoperability standards for AI systems across borders, particularly in cross-border digital trade, migration management, and health data systems, where fragmented AI governance creates friction and harm. Critically, the Dialogue can institutionalize a civil society and private sector engagement mechanism that goes beyond symbolic consultation. Africa's tech civil society - organizations working at the intersection of AI, gender, youth, and digital rights - must have a formal seat at the table in designing governance norms that affect their communities. Finally, the Dialogue can play a catalytic role in mobilizing funding for AI governance capacity in the Global South - supporting national regulators, universities, and civil society organizations to build the expertise needed to participate meaningfully in international AI governance, rather than simply receiving and implementing externally-designed frameworks.
column11: Several existing mechanisms provide a strong foundation the AI Dialogue should actively build upon. The ITU's AI for Good platform has cultivated a global network of AI stakeholders and should be formally connected to the Dialogue's outreach and participation infrastructure. UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) provides an already-ratified ethical framework that the Dialogue should reference as a baseline rather than starting from scratch on ethics. The Internet Governance Forum (IGF) and its Dynamic Coalitions on AI and Data Governance have built multi-stakeholder expertise over years and should be designated as a formal input mechanism to the Dialogue. The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and the Smart Africa Alliance represent key regional frameworks the Dialogue should explicitly integrate, ensuring that Africa's own governance priorities shape global norms rather than being retrofitted to them post-hoc. The UN Secretary-General's AI Advisory Body report also provides actionable recommendations the Dialogue should operationalize. The added value the AI Dialogue can uniquely bring is its universal UN membership legitimacy - giving it the convening authority to translate multi-stakeholder discussions into binding international commitments, which purely technical bodies like ITU or multi-stakeholder forums like IGF cannot do alone. The Dialogue should serve as the apex coordination mechanism that synthesizes these various threads into a coherent, action-oriented global AI governance architecture with clear accountability and implementation timelines.
column12: The AI Dialogue should adopt a multi-track participation model that meaningfully integrates government, civil society, private sector, academia, and technical communities - not as separate silos but as interdependent voices in a structured deliberative process. For civil society and community organizations, the Dialogue should establish a dedicated civil society forum running in parallel to the intergovernmental sessions, with a formal channel for civil society inputs to be tabled and responded to in plenary. This mirrors best practice from UNFCCC COP processes. For private sector participants, particularly small and medium-sized tech enterprises from the Global South, the Dialogue should create an innovation showcase and policy dialogue mechanism - ensuring that African AI startups and platforms like Shecode.ai can share real-world evidence of both the opportunities and governance failures they encounter. For academia, the Dialogue should commission thematic research briefs from universities in the Global South to provide evidence-based inputs that balance the often Northern-centric research base that dominates AI governance discourse. Structurally, sessions should be hybrid-first - enabling remote participation for stakeholders from developing countries who cannot travel to Geneva, with simultaneous interpretation available in UN languages plus key regional languages such as Swahili, Arabic, and Hausa. Dedicated capacity-building sessions before the main plenary would help equip stakeholders from low-resource settings to engage substantively with technical governance questions, rather than arriving unprepared and therefore disempowered.
column13: The most critically underrepresented voices in global AI governance are: women and girls, particularly those in the Global South; indigenous and rural communities whose languages, livelihoods, and cultural practices are being shaped by AI systems they had no role in designing; young people aged 18-35 in Africa, Asia, and Latin America who are simultaneously AI's most active users and most underrepresented in governance spaces; and persons with disabilities, who face acute AI-driven exclusion in digital service access. From my work with PAWA Initiative and Shecode.ai, I see daily how African women tech practitioners are excluded from global governance conversations not due to lack of expertise but due to structural barriers - visa restrictions that prevent travel to Geneva or New York, lack of funding to attend international forums, and online participation mechanisms that are poorly designed for low-bandwidth environments. To address this, the AI Dialogue should: establish a sponsored fellowship for civil society delegates from underrepresented regions and demographics to attend in person; create a digital participation platform optimized for low-bandwidth environments; partner with regional civil society networks across Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and Latin America to convene grassroots consultations whose outputs are formally submitted to the Dialogue; and mandate gender parity and regional diversity requirements for speakers and panelists in all sessions. Inclusion must be structural, not cosmetic - diversity in the room means nothing if the governance outcomes continue to reflect only the priorities of those who have historically dominated the conversation.
column14: To foster genuinely dynamic engagement, the AI Dialogue should move beyond the traditional plenary-and-panel format and experiment with several innovative models. First, thematic working groups with formal civil society co-chairs should be convened between sessions, producing substantive written recommendations rather than simply commenting on government-drafted texts. Second, a citizen and community testimony segment - modeled on human rights council mechanisms - should be embedded in each major session, where community representatives directly impacted by AI systems (women farmers using AI-based weather apps, gig workers managed by algorithmic platforms, students subject to AI proctoring tools) can give formal testimony that is entered into the official Dialogue record. Third, a real-time translation and accessibility protocol should be implemented, ensuring that participants from non-English-speaking regions can engage authentically in their preferred languages. Fourth, a pre-Dialogue grassroots consultation process - using mobile-first digital tools accessible even on low-data connections - should gather inputs from communities across the Global South, aggregated into regional position papers. Fifth, a youth-led side summit running in parallel to the main sessions would create a pipeline of next-generation AI governance voices and produce a Youth AI Governance Compact submitted formally to the plenary. These formats would transform the AI Dialogue from a diplomatic conference into a living, participatory governance process that reflects the full diversity of humanity's relationship with AI.
column15: Several promising practices and platforms deserve global attention as models for effective AI governance. Rwanda's National AI Policy and its focus on using AI for agricultural productivity and healthcare delivery in a resource-constrained context demonstrates that developing nations can be AI governance innovators, not just adopters. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has developed an AI policy framework with a dedicated Ethics and Governance pillar - providing a template for African nations seeking to build regulatory capacity. At the civil society level, the Algorithmic Justice League's work on auditing AI systems for gender and racial bias provides a practical methodology for bias detection that should be adopted as a global standard within AI governance frameworks. The Mozilla Foundation's Trustworthy AI program and its community-based research model demonstrates how civil society can produce credible, technically rigorous AI governance inputs. At the platform level, Shecode.ai's work in Nigeria on equipping women with AI literacy and entrepreneurship skills represents a grassroots approach to closing the AI gender gap that could be scaled with international support. The EU's AI Act, while imperfect, offers a risk-tiered regulatory approach that developing nations could adapt to their local contexts. The key lesson from all effective AI governance practices is that they are contextually grounded, multi-stakeholder in design, and adaptive over time - rather than one-size-fits-all frameworks imposed without local validation. The AI Dialogue should document, disseminate, and build upon these practices, creating a living repository of AI governance innovations from across all regions.

column2: Personería de Bogotá; Universidad Externado de Colombia
column5:
Consideramos exitoso el primer Diálogo Mundial sobre Gobernanza de la IA si logra pasar de una conversación general sobre riesgos y oportunidades a una agenda operativa, inclusiva y verificable.
En primer lugar, debería producir una hoja de ruta común que identifique prioridades, responsabilidades y mecanismos de seguimiento para los Estados, el sector privado, la academia, la sociedad civil y los organismos internacionales. En segundo lugar, el Diálogo debería consolidar estándares mínimos compartidos sobre transparencia, responsabilidad, supervisión humana, evaluación de riesgos y protección de derechos humanos, sin imponer un modelo único que desconozca las diferencias institucionales, culturales, lingüísticas y económicas de cada región.
También sería un éxito si permite cerrar brechas de participación: los países del Sur Global, las comunidades afectadas, las pequeñas organizaciones, los sistemas judiciales, los educadores y los usuarios finales no deben quedar como receptores pasivos de decisiones técnicas tomadas por pocos actores. La gobernanza de la IA debe construirse con evidencia científica, pero también con legitimidad democrática y sensibilidad social.
Finalmente, el Diálogo debería dejar resultados concretos en materia de desarrollo de capacidades: formación, alfabetización algorítmica, cooperación técnica, acceso a infraestructura, intercambio de buenas prácticas y criterios para el uso responsable de IA en sectores de alto impacto como justicia, educación, salud, servicios públicos y protección de poblaciones vulnerables.
El éxito no estaría solo en declarar principios, sino en crear condiciones para que la IA sea segura, confiable, explicable, respetuosa de los derechos humanos y útil para el desarrollo sostenible.
column6: Protection and promotion of human rights;Transparency, accountability, and human oversight;AI capacity-building;Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI
column7:
La selección responde a una preocupación central: la IA no debe gobernarse únicamente como una cuestión técnica, sino como una infraestructura social que incide en derechos, oportunidades, mercados, servicios públicos, educación, justicia y confianza institucional. Por ello, la protección y promoción de los derechos humanos debe ser el eje transversal. Sin este enfoque, la IA puede profundizar discriminaciones, excluir poblaciones vulnerables, afectar la privacidad, restringir libertades o producir decisiones automatizadas difíciles de controvertir.
La transparencia, la responsabilidad y la supervisión humana son igualmente urgentes porque permiten identificar quién diseña, entrena, implementa, audita y responde por los sistemas de IA. La supervisión humana significativa es indispensable en contextos de alto impacto, especialmente cuando las decisiones afectan salud, justicia, educación, empleo, seguridad social o acceso a servicios públicos.
El desarrollo de capacidades es prioritario porque existe una brecha entre quienes diseñan y controlan sistemas avanzados de IA y quienes apenas están construyendo marcos normativos, capacidades técnicas e infraestructura pública. Sin formación, alfabetización algorítmica, cooperación técnica y acceso equitativo a conocimiento, la gobernanza global puede reproducir desigualdades.
Finalmente, las implicaciones sociales, económicas, éticas, culturales, lingüísticas y técnicas deben abordarse de manera integral. En América Latina y otros contextos diversos, los sistemas de IA pueden fallar si no comprenden idiomas, territorios, formas de exclusión, realidades institucionales y diferencias culturales. La gobernanza debe reconocer que la IA no impacta a todas las sociedades de la misma manera; por eso requiere enfoques diferenciales, inclusivos y sensibles al contexto.
column8:
Sí. Aunque los temas identificados son amplios, considero importante reforzar algunas cuestiones transversales. La primera es la justicia algorítmica en contextos de desigualdad estructural. No basta con hablar de derechos humanos en abstracto; es necesario evaluar cómo los sistemas de IA afectan de forma diferenciada a mujeres, niñas, comunidades rurales, personas mayores, personas con discapacidad, pueblos indígenas, migrantes, víctimas de violencia y grupos históricamente excluidos.
La segunda cuestión es la responsabilidad de las plataformas y empresas que diseñan, distribuyen o amplifican sistemas de IA. La gobernanza global debe evitar que la “neutralidad tecnológica” se utilice para trasladar los costos del daño a los usuarios, consumidores, trabajadores o instituciones públicas. Esto exige reglas sobre trazabilidad, auditoría, documentación, gestión de riesgos, reparación y rendición de cuentas.
La tercera cuestión es el impacto de la IA en la justicia, la administración pública y la democracia. Los sistemas automatizados pueden mejorar eficiencia, pero también afectar debido proceso, acceso a la información, participación ciudadana, confianza pública y control institucional. Por ello se requieren estándares específicos para usos públicos de IA, especialmente cuando estén involucradas decisiones estatales o servicios esenciales.
La cuarta cuestión es la sostenibilidad ambiental y material de la IA. La discusión sobre gobernanza debe incluir consumo energético, concentración de infraestructura, uso de agua, dependencia tecnológica y cadenas globales de suministro.
Finalmente, debería incorporarse la educación ciudadana en IA como condición democrática: las personas deben comprender cuándo interactúan con IA, cómo se usan sus datos, qué riesgos existen y qué mecanismos tienen para reclamar, corregir o impugnar decisiones automatizadas.
column9:
En Colombia y América Latina, las brechas de gobernanza de la IA están afectando especialmente al sector público, jurídico, educativo y empresarial.
El principal reto es que la adopción de herramientas de IA avanza más rápido que las capacidades institucionales para regularlas, auditarlas y usarlas de manera transparente. Esto puede generar riesgos en derechos fundamentales, protección de datos, igualdad, debido proceso, acceso a servicios públicos y confianza ciudadana.
En el sector jurídico y público, la IA ofrece oportunidades importantes para mejorar la eficiencia administrativa, orientar ciudadanos, clasificar información, apoyar la redacción de documentos, fortalecer la investigación jurídica y reducir barreras de acceso a la justicia. Sin embargo, si no existen reglas claras sobre supervisión humana, trazabilidad, responsabilidad y calidad de los datos, pueden producirse decisiones opacas, sesgadas o difíciles de controvertir.
Otra brecha relevante es la desigualdad territorial y educativa. Las grandes ciudades, universidades y empresas con mayor capacidad tecnológica pueden aprovechar antes la IA, mientras que municipios, comunidades rurales, pequeñas entidades públicas y organizaciones sociales quedan rezagadas. Esto exige programas de formación, alfabetización algorítmica, infraestructura digital y cooperación técnica.
También existe un reto cultural y lingüístico: muchos sistemas de IA no comprenden adecuadamente los contextos locales, los lenguajes jurídicos nacionales, las realidades regionales ni las necesidades de comunidades vulnerables. Allí surge una oportunidad: desarrollar modelos, datos y aplicaciones ajustadas al contexto latinoamericano, con enfoque de derechos humanos, inclusión, diversidad cultural y sostenibilidad.
En síntesis, la IA puede ser una herramienta de transformación institucional y social, pero solo si la gobernanza logra equilibrar innovación, confianza pública, responsabilidad empresarial, protección de derechos y desarrollo de capacidades.
column10:
El Diálogo sobre IA puede desempeñar un papel decisivo como espacio de coordinación política, técnica y ética entre Estados, organismos multilaterales, sector privado, academia, sociedad civil y comunidades afectadas. Su principal aporte sería reducir la fragmentación actual de la gobernanza de la IA, en la que distintos países y regiones avanzan con reglas, estándares y capacidades desiguales.
En primer lugar, el Diálogo puede construir un lenguaje común sobre IA segura, fiable, transparente y respetuosa de los derechos humanos. Esto permitiría que las discusiones no se limiten a los países con mayor capacidad tecnológica, sino que integren las prioridades del Sur Global, los países en desarrollo y los sectores sociales que suelen quedar por fuera de las decisiones técnicas. La página oficial del Diálogo destaca precisamente que su finalidad es que la gobernanza refleje las prioridades de todas las naciones, no solo de las más avanzadas tecnológicamente.
En segundo lugar, puede impulsar cooperación internacional mediante intercambio de buenas prácticas, asistencia técnica, formación, infraestructura, investigación compartida y mecanismos para cerrar brechas digitales y de capacidades. Esto es especialmente relevante para América Latina, donde la adopción de IA avanza más rápido que la capacidad institucional para auditarla, explicarla y regularla.
En tercer lugar, el Diálogo puede servir como puente entre la evidencia científica y la toma de decisiones públicas, articulándose con el Panel Científico Internacional Independiente sobre IA previsto por la Resolución 79/325.
Finalmente, su valor estaría en promover compromisos concretos: estándares mínimos de supervisión humana, transparencia, responsabilidad, protección de datos, evaluación de riesgos, inclusión lingüística y cultural, y reparación frente a daños. Así, la cooperación internacional no sería solo declarativa, sino orientada a resultados verificables, desarrollo sostenible y protección efectiva de las personas.
column11:
El Diálogo sobre IA debería apoyarse en iniciativas ya existentes para evitar duplicidades y construir una gobernanza global más coherente. Entre ellas se destacan la Recomendación sobre la Ética de la IA de la UNESCO, que ofrece un marco centrado en dignidad humana, derechos, transparencia, equidad y supervisión humana, aplicable a todos los Estados miembros de la organización.
También debería conectarse con los Principios de IA de la OCDE, adoptados en 2019 y actualizados en 2024, que promueven una IA confiable, innovadora, respetuosa de los derechos humanos y útil como base para la cooperación internacional. En esa misma línea, la Alianza Global sobre Inteligencia Artificial —GPAI—, integrada con la OCDE, aporta una comunidad multiactor de expertos, gobiernos y regiones para avanzar en IA segura, confiable y centrada en las personas.
El Diálogo también debería articularse con el Proceso de Hiroshima del G7, especialmente con su Código Internacional de Conducta para sistemas avanzados de IA, que promueve medidas de gestión de riesgos durante todo el ciclo de vida de los sistemas. Igualmente, podría aprovechar el marco de reporte de la OCDE sobre dicho Código, orientado a generar información comparable sobre evaluación de riesgos, incidentes y prácticas de transparencia.
Su valor añadido estaría en ampliar la legitimidad y la inclusión. Muchas iniciativas actuales han sido lideradas por países con alta capacidad tecnológica. El Diálogo puede convertirse en el espacio donde el Sur Global, América Latina, comunidades afectadas, academia, sociedad civil, pequeñas empresas y entidades públicas participen en igualdad de condiciones.
Además, puede conectar principios dispersos con compromisos prácticos: desarrollo de capacidades, cooperación técnica, interoperabilidad normativa, protección de derechos humanos, estándares de supervisión humana y mecanismos de seguimiento. Así, el Diálogo no reemplazaría lo existente, sino que lo ordenaría, democratizaría y orientaría hacia resultados verificables.
column12:
Las distintas partes implicadas pueden contribuir al Diálogo sobre IA desde sus capacidades y responsabilidades específicas. Los Estados pueden aportar marcos normativos, experiencias regulatorias, políticas públicas, necesidades de cooperación técnica y criterios para proteger derechos humanos en sectores sensibles. Los organismos internacionales pueden facilitar metodologías comunes, asistencia técnica, indicadores y espacios de coordinación entre regiones. El sector privado debe compartir buenas prácticas sobre gestión de riesgos, documentación, auditoría, transparencia, seguridad, trazabilidad y reparación frente a daños. La academia y los centros de investigación pueden aportar evidencia científica independiente, análisis comparado, metodologías de evaluación y estudios sobre impactos sociales, económicos, culturales y técnicos. La sociedad civil, las comunidades afectadas y los usuarios finales deben tener un papel central para visibilizar riesgos reales, exclusiones, barreras territoriales, discriminación algorítmica y necesidades de participación democrática.
Recomendaríamos que el Diálogo tenga una estructura multiactor, regionalmente equilibrada y orientada a resultados. No debería limitarse a paneles generales, sino combinar sesiones plenarias con mesas temáticas de trabajo sobre derechos humanos, supervisión humana, desarrollo de capacidades, gobernanza interoperable, datos, modelos abiertos, seguridad y usos de IA en sectores de alto impacto.
También sería útil crear espacios regionales preparatorios, especialmente para América Latina, África, Asia y pequeños Estados insulares, de manera que las prioridades del Sur Global no lleguen fragmentadas. El formato debería incluir consultas públicas, participación virtual, documentos breves de posición, relatorías por tema y mecanismos de seguimiento posterior.
La estructura ideal sería: primero, identificación de brechas; segundo, intercambio de experiencias; tercero, formulación de compromisos; cuarto, definición de indicadores; y quinto, revisión periódica. Así, el Diálogo pasaría de la deliberación a la cooperación práctica, con resultados verificables, lenguaje accesible y participación significativa de actores que no siempre están presentes en la gobernanza tecnológica global.
column13:
En los debates mundiales sobre gobernanza de la IA siguen estando subrepresentadas varias voces esenciales. En primer lugar, las comunidades del Sur Global, especialmente América Latina, África, Asia y pequeños Estados insulares, que muchas veces participan como receptoras de tecnologías diseñadas en otros contextos, pero no como actoras principales en la definición de reglas, estándares y prioridades.
También están subrepresentadas las comunidades rurales, pueblos indígenas, comunidades afrodescendientes, mujeres, niñas, personas mayores, personas con discapacidad, migrantes, víctimas de violencia, trabajadores afectados por la automatización y usuarios de servicios públicos. Estas poblaciones pueden sufrir impactos diferenciados por sistemas de IA que no reconocen sus lenguas, culturas, territorios, condiciones socioeconómicas o barreras de acceso digital.
En el sector público y jurídico, también deberían escucharse más las voces de jueces, defensores públicos, consultorios jurídicos, personerías, organizaciones de derechos humanos y entidades territoriales que enfrentan directamente problemas de acceso a la justicia, salud, educación y protección social. La gobernanza de la IA no puede quedar concentrada en grandes empresas tecnológicas, expertos técnicos o gobiernos con alta capacidad institucional.
Para incluir estas voces, el Diálogo debería crear mecanismos reales de participación: consultas regionales, espacios virtuales multilingües, becas de participación, documentos en lenguaje claro, relatorías temáticas, mesas con comunidades afectadas y canales para recibir experiencias locales. También se deben financiar procesos de formación previa, porque participar en gobernanza tecnológica exige capacidades mínimas de comprensión técnica, jurídica y ética.
La inclusión no debe ser simbólica. Las comunidades subrepresentadas deben poder influir en la agenda, formular recomendaciones, revisar documentos finales y participar en los mecanismos de seguimiento. Solo así la gobernanza global de la IA será legítima, democrática y sensible a los impactos reales de la tecnología.
column14:
Para fomentar un compromiso significativo y dinámico, el Diálogo sobre IA debería combinar formatos deliberativos, técnicos, pedagógicos y participativos. Un primer formato innovador serían los laboratorios regionales de gobernanza, en los que actores de América Latina, África, Asia, Europa y pequeños Estados insulares trabajen sobre casos concretos de uso de IA en justicia, salud, educación, empleo, servicios públicos y plataformas digitales. Esto permitiría pasar de principios abstractos a problemas reales.
También serían útiles las clínicas de casos, donde comunidades afectadas, entidades públicas, empresas, academia y sociedad civil analicen situaciones específicas de daño algorítmico, exclusión digital, sesgos, falta de transparencia o uso de IA en decisiones públicas. Estas clínicas podrían producir recomendaciones prácticas sobre reparación, auditoría, supervisión humana y prevención de riesgos.
Otro formato relevante serían las simulaciones de gobernanza, similares a ejercicios de negociación multiactor, en las que los participantes asuman roles de Estados, empresas, usuarios, comunidades vulnerables, jueces, reguladores y organizaciones sociales. Esto ayudaría a comprender tensiones entre innovación, seguridad, derechos humanos, competitividad y responsabilidad.
El Diálogo también podría incorporar consultas ciudadanas multilingües en línea, con lenguaje claro, herramientas visuales, formularios breves, videos explicativos y espacios asincrónicos para quienes no puedan asistir presencialmente. Además, deberían existir mesas juveniles, comunitarias y territoriales, con apoyo económico y técnico para garantizar participación real.
Finalmente, proponemos usar prototipos de políticas públicas y sandboxes regulatorios deliberativos, donde se diseñen, prueben y evalúen marcos de transparencia, evaluación de riesgos, rendición de cuentas y supervisión humana. El valor de estos formatos está en que convierten el Diálogo en un proceso vivo: no solo escuchar intervenciones, sino construir soluciones, contrastarlas con evidencia y revisar su impacto con participación amplia.
column15:
El Diálogo sobre IA debería apoyarse en políticas y enfoques que ya ofrecen herramientas concretas de gobernanza. Un primer referente es la Recomendación sobre la Ética de la IA de la UNESCO, por su enfoque centrado en derechos humanos, dignidad, transparencia, equidad y supervisión humana, aplicable a los Estados miembros.
También es relevante el NIST AI Risk Management Framework, que propone una metodología práctica para identificar, medir, gestionar y monitorear riesgos de IA durante el ciclo de vida de los sistemas. Este enfoque puede servir para entidades públicas, empresas, universidades y organizaciones sociales que necesitan pasar de principios generales a controles verificables.
Otro ejemplo es el Reglamento Europeo de Inteligencia Artificial, que adopta una lógica basada en niveles de riesgo y fija obligaciones diferenciadas para desarrolladores y usuarios de sistemas de IA, especialmente en usos de alto impacto.
En el caso colombiano, la Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial —CONPES 4144 de 2025— constituye una plataforma útil porque reconoce la necesidad de articular Estado, academia, sector privado y ciudadanía para promover adopción responsable, capacidades nacionales e innovación.
Como enfoques prácticos, destacaría: evaluaciones de impacto algorítmico, auditorías independientes, registros públicos de sistemas de IA usados por el Estado, sandboxes regulatorios, alfabetización algorítmica, protocolos de supervisión humana, mecanismos de queja y reparación, y compras públicas responsables de IA.
El valor añadido del Diálogo sería conectar estos instrumentos, evitar duplicidades y traducirlos en cooperación internacional, asistencia técnica, estándares mínimos comunes y mecanismos de seguimiento. Así, las buenas prácticas no quedarían aisladas en países o sectores con mayor capacidad, sino que podrían adaptarse a contextos como América Latina, con enfoque de derechos humanos, inclusión territorial y desarrollo sostenible.

column5:
A successful first Global Dialogue on AI Governance would deliver concrete, inclusive, and action-oriented outcomes that bridge global policy with local realities.
First, the Dialogue should establish a shared global framework for responsible AI governance, grounded in human rights, ethical standards, and equitable access. This framework must be adaptable to different socio-economic contexts, particularly in the Global South.
Second, success would be measured by meaningful inclusion of underrepresented voices, especially youth, women, and actors from developing countries. Ensuring their participation in both decision-making and implementation processes is essential to avoid widening global inequalities.
Third, the Dialogue should catalyze practical commitments—including financing mechanisms, partnerships, and capacity-building initiatives—that support countries and grassroots organizations in safely adopting and governing AI technologies.
Additionally, the creation of knowledge-sharing platforms and South-South cooperation mechanisms would enable the exchange of best practices and locally relevant solutions.
Finally, a clear roadmap with measurable milestones leading to the 2027 Dialogue should be adopted, ensuring continuity, accountability, and sustained global engagement.
For Phoenix Revival Association, success means moving beyond dialogue to transformative action, where AI governance becomes a tool for inclusive economic development, peacebuilding, and sustainable livelihoods, particularly for women and youth.

column7:
Phoenix Revival Association prioritizes these thematic areas because they directly address the structural inequalities and governance gaps faced by communities in developing contexts.
AI capacity-building is critical to ensure that women and youth are not only consumers of AI but active creators and decision-makers. Without targeted investment in skills development, the digital divide will continue to widen.
Protection and promotion of human rights is central to preventing the misuse of AI technologies, particularly in fragile or politically sensitive environments. AI systems must uphold dignity, equity, and non-discrimination.
Transparency, accountability, and human oversight are essential to building public trust. In many communities, limited awareness of AI systems increases vulnerability to bias and manipulation. Clear accountability mechanisms are therefore crucial.
Finally, addressing the social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic, and technical implications of AI ensures that governance frameworks are context-sensitive. In Africa, for example, linguistic diversity and informal economies require tailored AI solutions that reflect local realities.
Together, these priorities enable a holistic and inclusive approach to AI governance, ensuring that technological advancement translates into equitable development outcomes.
column8:
One critical cross-cutting issue is the risk of deepening global inequality through uneven AI access and infrastructure gaps. Many developing countries lack the digital infrastructure, data ecosystems, and regulatory capacity needed to fully participate in the AI economy.
Another emerging concern is the intersection of AI and peacebuilding. In fragile contexts, AI can either mitigate or exacerbate conflict, depending on how it is governed. There is a need for frameworks that explicitly integrate AI into peace and security strategies, particularly in regions facing electoral tensions or social fragmentation.
Additionally, data sovereignty and ownership remain underexplored. Communities and countries must have greater control over how their data is collected, used, and monetized, to prevent exploitation and ensure fair value distribution.
The environmental impact of AI systems is also an urgent issue. The energy consumption associated with large-scale AI models raises sustainability concerns, particularly for countries already vulnerable to climate change.
Finally, there is a growing need to address AI literacy and public awareness as a governance issue. Empowering citizens to understand and critically engage with AI systems is essential for democratic participation and accountability.
Addressing these cross-cutting issues will ensure that AI governance is not only technically robust but also equitable, sustainable, and responsive to global challenges.
column9:
In Cameroon and across Sub-Saharan Africa, governance gaps in AI are already shaping both risks and opportunities for inclusive development.
A major challenge lies in limited AI capacity and infrastructure. While interest in AI is growing, there is a shortage of skilled professionals, localized data, and institutional readiness. This constrains governments, civil society, and youth-led organizations from meaningfully participating in AI development and governance, reinforcing dependency on external technologies.
Another critical gap is the absence of comprehensive regulatory frameworks. Without clear policies on data protection, algorithmic accountability, and ethical standards, communities are exposed to risks such as biased AI systems, misinformation, and misuse in sensitive contexts like elections. This directly impacts human rights, transparency, and public trust.
Additionally, linguistic and cultural underrepresentation remains a major issue. Many AI systems do not reflect African languages or socio-cultural realities, limiting accessibility and relevance for local populations, particularly in informal and rural settings.
However, these gaps also present significant opportunities. There is strong potential to leapfrog traditional development pathways by integrating AI into education, entrepreneurship, and public service delivery. With targeted capacity-building initiatives, youth and women can become drivers of innovation, job creation, and digital governance.
Furthermore, the current stage offers an opportunity to co-create context-specific AI governance models that prioritize ethics, inclusion, and sustainability from the outset rather than retrofitting regulations after harm occurs.
For Phoenix Revival Association, these dynamics reinforce the urgency of investing in AI literacy, inclusive innovation ecosystems, and community centered governance approaches, ensuring that AI becomes a tool for empowerment, peacebuilding, and equitable economic growth rather than a source of exclusion.
column10:
The AI Dialogue can serve as a global coordination and trust-building platform that bridges fragmented governance efforts and fosters inclusive multilateral cooperation.
First, it can harmonize principles and standards by aligning national and regional AI policies with globally shared values such as human rights, accountability, and equity, while respecting contextual diversity.
Second, the Dialogue can promote North–South and South–South cooperation, enabling knowledge exchange, technical assistance, and resource-sharing. This is essential for ensuring that developing countries are not left behind in shaping and benefiting from AI governance frameworks.
Third, it can catalyze multi-stakeholder partnerships by connecting governments, civil society, academia, and the private sector to co-create practical solutions, including capacity-building programs, regulatory sandboxes, and ethical AI tools.
Additionally, the Dialogue can function as a mechanism for collective accountability, tracking commitments and progress across countries and institutions.
For Phoenix Revival Association, the AI Dialogue is an opportunity to ensure that grassroots perspectives inform global decisions, and that international cooperation translates into tangible support for local innovation ecosystems, youth empowerment, and inclusive economic development.
column11:
The AI Dialogue should build upon existing global and regional initiatives such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the OECD AI Principles, the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI), and emerging African frameworks including the African Union AI Strategy.
It should also connect with multi-stakeholder platforms, open-source communities, and grassroots initiatives that are already advancing AI literacy, ethical innovation, and digital inclusion.
The added value of the AI Dialogue lies in its ability to convene these fragmented efforts under a unified, inclusive UN platform, ensuring coherence and reducing duplication.
Furthermore, the Dialogue can elevate voices from the Global South, which are often underrepresented in existing initiatives, and facilitate practical implementation pathways by linking policy discussions with funding, capacity-building, and technical support.
Another key contribution is the creation of a continuous global feedback loop, where lessons learned from local implementation inform global standards, making governance more adaptive and responsive.
For Phoenix Revival Association, the Dialogue’s value is in transforming existing commitments into coordinated, actionable outcomes that directly benefit underserved communities.
column12:
Effective AI governance requires inclusive, structured, and participatory engagement from all stakeholders.
Governments can contribute by sharing policy experiences, committing to ethical standards, and supporting regulatory alignment. Civil society organizations can provide community insights, accountability mechanisms, and advocacy for human rights. The private sector can contribute technical expertise, innovation, and responsible business practices, while academia can support research, evidence-building, and capacity development.
To maximize impact, the AI Dialogue should adopt a hybrid, multi-layered structure:
•High-level plenaries for political commitment and global alignment
•Thematic working groups for deep technical and policy discussions
•Regional consultations to reflect diverse contexts
•Youth and civil society forums to ensure inclusive participation
Additionally, the Dialogue should integrate year-round engagement mechanisms, including virtual platforms, policy labs, and collaborative networks, ensuring continuity beyond annual meetings.
Clear outputs such as policy recommendations, partnership frameworks, and measurable action plans should be defined for each session.
Phoenix Revival Association recommends a format that prioritizes co-creation over consultation, ensuring that all stakeholders actively shape outcomes rather than passively contribute.
column13:
Global AI governance discussions often underrepresent youth, women, grassroots organizations, and communities from developing countries, particularly in Africa. Additionally, linguistic minorities, rural populations, and informal sector actors are rarely included, despite being significantly impacted by AI systems.
This exclusion risks creating governance frameworks that are detached from lived realities, reinforcing inequality and limiting the effectiveness of AI policies.
To address this, the AI Dialogue should implement intentional inclusion mechanisms, such as:
•Dedicated quotas or participation targets for underrepresented groups
•Financial support (travel grants, stipends) to enable participation
•Multilingual engagement to overcome language barriers
•Partnerships with local organizations to identify and elevate community voices
•Digital participation tools should also be leveraged to ensure accessible, remote engagement, particularly for those unable to attend in person.
Furthermore, integrating youth-led and community-driven consultations into the official Dialogue process will ensure that diverse perspectives shape outcomes from the ground up.
For Phoenix Revival Association, inclusive participation is not optional—it is essential for building equitable, legitimate, and sustainable AI governance systems.
column14:
To foster meaningful engagement, the AI Dialogue should adopt interactive and solution-oriented formats that go beyond traditional panel discussions.
Key innovative approaches include:
•Policy hackathons, where diverse stakeholders co-create governance solutions in real time
•Simulation exercises, allowing participants to explore the impacts of AI policies in different scenarios (e.g., elections, healthcare, education)
•AI governance labs, focused on testing regulatory approaches and ethical frameworks
•Storytelling and community showcases, highlighting real-world experiences and grassroots innovations
Additionally, digital collaboration platforms can enable continuous participation before, during, and after the Dialogue, allowing stakeholders to contribute ideas, vote on priorities, and track progress.
Youth-led sessions and intergenerational dialogues can also foster fresh perspectives and bridge knowledge gaps.
The Dialogue should prioritize participatory methods that encourage co-creation, peer learning, and practical problem solving.
For Phoenix Revival Association, these formats are essential to ensure that the Dialogue is not only informative but also transformative, generating actionable solutions that reflect diverse global realities.
column15:
Several existing policies and practices offer valuable lessons for effective AI governance.
The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI provides a comprehensive global framework grounded in human rights, inclusivity, and sustainability. Similarly, the OECD AI Principles emphasize transparency, accountability, and robustness, influencing national policies worldwide.
The European Union’s AI Act demonstrates a risk based regulatory approach, offering practical mechanisms for classifying and managing AI systems based on their potential impact.
In Africa, emerging initiatives such as national AI strategies and the African Union’s digital transformation agenda highlight the importance of context-specific governance frameworks.
At the grassroots level, community-based approaches such as AI literacy programs, youth innovation hubs, and open-data initiatives are critical for democratizing access and building local capacity.
Public-private partnerships have also proven effective in advancing responsible AI innovation, particularly when aligned with ethical standards and inclusive development goals.
Phoenix Revival Association contributes through AI education, youth empowerment, and community centered innovation programs, demonstrating how local actors can operationalize global principles.
These examples show that effective AI governance requires a multi-level approach, combining global standards, national policies, and community-driven implementation to ensure that AI benefits all.

column7:
At Plan C we're responding to the problem of AI answers on leading platforms (chatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Google) containing misinformation and omissions, and leading a project to coordinate content improvements across high-authority abortion websites to improve answers from the source. These strategies are distinct but complementary to efforts around policy change, addressing bias and privacy/security. From the beginning 10y ago, Plan C has prioritized SEO and search visibility because of a) the censorship we've always experienced in sharing this health information online, and b) our understanding of the importance of an accurate and complete online search journey, as we introduced the concept of safe self-managed abortion in health systems and culture.  

We’re also tracking research to understand if and how answers improve with on-page content and structure changes, building and using feedback loops with AI companies, forging relationships to address new issues as they arise, and sharing AI Optimization best practices and learnings with the reproductive health and access movement.
column8: I think the emergent issue of accuracy, completeness and censorship of information on leading AI answer & summary platforms is captured by a few of the above points.
column9:
In the US, search is an extremely common way to learn about reproductive health options and make informed choices about care. Google searches used to contain lists of URLs, including manipulative SEO content and “fake clinic” listings. This required the searcher to parse through resources. Now people often seek information on platforms like ChatGPT and Claude, or see AI Overviews at the top of Google results. Google search summaries are seen by 2B people/month, and and 25% of ChatGPT’s 900M users/week are asking health questions. 

AI answers can be helpful, even better than traditional search - but right now, they can contain misinformation and omissions. As more people turn to AI for abortion information, answers are often incomplete or inaccurate – and this can be life-altering. A recent UPenn study found that only 73% of medication abortion answers were accurate. Only 56% were accurate on ChatGPT. And responses were disproportionately inaccurate in abortion-restrictive states. Medication abortion, a rapidly-growing option for tens of millions of people of reproductive age living in restricted states, showed the highest variability across models. What someone sees in their moment of search can be life-altering. 

Why it's happening? Models are synthesizing answers and interpreting legal risk and clinic access, based on what’s found on the open internet. This can lead to errors and omissions in the options and resources platforms include.  

We’re optimistic that this experience can be even better for abortion seekers than old methods of searching online, but it’s not going to happen organically. AI could represent a complete breakthrough in access to accurate, helpful and human-centered information pathways. Potentially millions of people will have a clearer more complete understanding of abortion options in their area (UPenn estimates 1.3M pregnant people across the US are currently at risk of encountering misinformation on AI platforms annually). Abortion stigma will be lessened, by factual no-nonsense answers to questions are served by leading AI platforms treating this as any other information. Groups like Plan C are designing strategies to improve on-page information, opening conversations with experts and AI companies that center accuracy and trust of the tools, and researching answers to understand how things shift and change and respond accordingly. Other groups are taking other approaches to improve accuracy, shape training and reinforce policy, privacy and anti-bias goals. We see this as an “all hands on deck” moment to act, while these tools hit the market and protocol gets established.

These strategies are distinct but complementary to efforts around policy change, addressing bias and privacy/security. We’re also tracking research via partners regularly testing prompts on these platforms, to understand if and how answers improve with on-page content and structure changes. We're building and using feedback loops with AI companies, forging relationships to address new issues as they arise, and sharing AI Optimization best practices and learnings with the reproductive health and access movement. We're most interested in answers generated on leading answer and summary platforms, because this is where we can reach a broad swath of the public, adopting these mainstream tools (or continuing to use google but relying on the AI summary) and using the tools for their health answer capabilities. We know this is already very common: 25% of chatGPT's 900m/week prompts are health related, and a recent Rock+Health study found that up to 1/3 of all prompts on leading platforms are health related: http://rockhealth.com/insights/the-tortoise-and-the-hare-of-care-health-ai-insights-from-rock-healths-2025-consumer-adoption-survey/  We're specifically starting with content areas that are historically under-explained or left vague, because of the nature of the abortion issue (sensitivity/privacy/complexity) and adding nuance and depth to details that commonly shape repro health answers.

column5:
A successful Dialogue would produce three things: shared language, a monitoring commitment, and a mandate for independent oversight.
My EU-funded audit of six major AI systems found that the same model can deliver accurate information in one language and propaganda-aligned content in another. This is measurable today with open methodology. The Dialogue should endorse repeatable, multilingual benchmarking as a baseline expectation for high-risk contexts, and commit to independent auditing as the standard â€” not self-reporting by developers.
A concrete success would be agreement that language-specific safety evaluation is a condition for public-sector AI procurement.
