column7: These choices focus on control points that shape the system, not just its outcomes. Interoperability matters because fragmented regimes will create conflict, arbitrage, and uneven power, so alignment across jurisdictions is a first-order need. Capacity-building is non-negotiable because without technical and institutional capability, most actors remain rule-takers, not participants. Transparency, accountability, and human oversight turn intent into enforcement, making AI systems auditable, contestable, and governable in practice. Open-source, open data, and open models determine how power and access are distributed, reducing concentration and enabling broader innovation. Taken together, this set builds a coherent stack: align governance, expand participation, enforce responsibility, and distribute capability.
column8:
Yes. A key gap is the absence of QA/QC standards for AI model weights and guardrails. Current discussions focus on outcomes and principles, but not enough on the integrity of the artifacts that actually drive behavior. Model weights are the executable core of an AI system. Yet there is no widely accepted framework for validating their provenance, testing their failure modes, or certifying their safety before and after deployment. This creates blind spots where unsafe behaviors can persist even when high-level policies exist.
In parallel, guardrail standards remain inconsistent and opaque. Systems are being deployed with safety layers that vary widely in design, rigor, and auditability. Without shared benchmarks for robustness, red-teaming, and adversarial resilience, it is difficult to compare systems or ensure minimum safety thresholds across contexts.
An emerging concern is what can be described as AI-induced cognitive harm, including forms of over-reliance, distorted reasoning patterns, or â€œAI psychosisâ€ in extreme cases of prolonged interaction with unstable or misaligned systems. These risks sit between technical safety and human impact, but are not cleanly captured under existing themes. They require new evaluation methods that combine behavioral testing, longitudinal user studies, and system-level audits.
Addressing these gaps would mean treating AI systems more like critical infrastructure: defining testable QA/QC pipelines for weights, standardizing guardrail performance metrics, and establishing post-deployment monitoring for cognitive and societal effects. Without this layer, governance remains high-level while risk accumulates at the level where systems actually operate.
column9:
Governance gaps are already visible in how guardrails fail under real-world conditions, even in systems built and deployed in the United States. Cases like Adam Raine highlight that current safety layers are not consistently robust, especially when users engage systems in prolonged or psychologically sensitive contexts. This exposes a deeper issue: guardrails are often designed within a narrow socio-cultural frame, yet deployed at global scale.
In a country like India, this gap becomes more pronounced. The population is highly diverse across language, culture, and socio-economic conditions. A large share of users are young adults, which increases exposure to systems that may not be calibrated for local contexts or vulnerabilities. As a result, risks such as cognitive over-reliance, misinterpretation of outputs, or unsafe behavioral influence are likely to scale faster and with less institutional buffering than in more homogeneous or resource-rich settings.
A second challenge is economic anxiety linked to job displacement. The pace of AI adoption is outpacing the development of reskilling infrastructure and labor transition frameworks. This creates uncertainty, particularly in service-driven sectors, where automation is both visible and immediate. Without credible pathways for workforce adaptation, trust in AI systems and governance frameworks may erode.
A third issue is hallucination and output validity. In high-volume information environments, unreliable outputs can amplify misinformation and reduce the signal quality of public discourse. This is especially critical in regions where digital literacy varies widely.
At the same time, there is opportunity. These gaps create pressure to build context-aware guardrails, stronger validation standards, and localized governance models that can better reflect the realities of diverse, high-growth digital societies.
column10:
The AI Dialogue can act as a coordination layer that turns fragmented national efforts into a minimally aligned global system. Its role is not to impose uniform rules, but to create shared reference points that different jurisdictions can map to. This is most critical for interoperability, where mutual recognition of standards can reduce regulatory conflict while preserving local autonomy.
It can also anchor baseline operational standards. Today, most cooperation sits at the level of principles. The Dialogue can push convergence toward testable elements such as auditability, guardrail robustness, and early QA/QC norms for model weights. Even partial alignment here would improve comparability and trust across systems.
A second role is to rebalance participation. Many countries lack the infrastructure and institutional capacity to engage meaningfully in AI governance. The Dialogue can connect policy discussions with capacity-building mechanisms, ensuring that standards are not defined by a narrow set of actors. This strengthens legitimacy and reduces long-term fragmentation.
Third, it can function as a structured interface between states and technical actors. AI systems are built outside government, so governance that excludes developers and researchers will remain abstract. The Dialogue can formalize how technical insight feeds into policy design without collapsing into industry capture.
Finally, it can establish continuity and accountability. Regular cycles of reporting, benchmarking, and review create pressure to move from intent to implementation. Progress becomes visible, gaps become comparable, and cooperation becomes iterative rather than episodic.
If it performs these roles, the Dialogue shifts from a forum of exchange to an early-stage governance infrastructure. That is where international cooperation starts to compound.
column11:
The AI Dialogue should build on existing efforts that already shape norms, standards, and coordination, rather than duplicating them. Key anchors include the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, and technical standard-setting bodies such as ISO and IEEE. It should also connect with multi-stakeholder safety efforts like the AI Safety Institute and development-focused platforms under the United Nations system.
The added value of the AI Dialogue is not another set of principles, but integration and translation. First, it can map these frameworks against each other to identify overlaps, gaps, and points of divergence, creating a usable layer of interoperability across regimes. Second, it can translate high-level norms into baseline operational expectations, especially around auditability, guardrails, and early QA/QC standards, without replacing the role of technical bodies.
Third, it can act as a bridge between policy and implementation. Many initiatives remain siloed, with limited feedback loops between standard-setters, governments, and developers. The Dialogue can formalize this interface, ensuring that technical constraints and governance goals evolve together.
Fourth, it can extend inclusion by linking these initiatives to capacity-building pathways for countries currently underrepresented in standard-setting processes. This reduces the risk of norms being globally applied but locally misaligned.
In effect, the Dialogueâ€™s value lies in stitching together a fragmented landscape into a minimally coherent system, where cooperation becomes cumulative rather than duplicative.
column12:
Different stakeholders should contribute based on what they control in the system, not just their formal roles.
Governments should define policy priorities, commit to interoperable approaches, and provide public accountability on implementation.
Industry should contribute technical evidence, disclose system limitations, and participate in defining testable standards for guardrails and auditability.
Academia and research institutions should lead on independent evaluation, red-teaming, and long-horizon risk analysis.
Civil society should surface user-level harms, cultural context, and rights-based concerns that are often missed in system design.
Standards bodies should translate these inputs into measurable benchmarks and certification pathways.
For structure, the Dialogue should move from open discussion to focused, output-driven modules.
First, organize around thematic working tracks aligned to priority control points such as interoperability, accountability, capacity-building, and openness. Each track should have a clear mandate and defined outputs per cycle.
Second, adopt a two-layer format:
a high-level plenary for alignment and political signaling
smaller technical working groups for drafting standards, frameworks, and mappings
Third, require pre-submitted evidence and position papers. This reduces generic statements and anchors discussions in concrete proposals.
Fourth, introduce iterative cycles. Each Dialogue should review progress against prior commitments, update benchmarks, and publish a concise outcome document with defined next steps and responsible actors.
Fifth, ensure structured inclusion of technical actors through formal interfaces, not ad hoc participation, so that policy remains grounded in system realities.
Finally, embed capacity-building linkages into each track, so that outputs are paired with pathways for adoption across different regions.
This structure keeps the Dialogue practical, comparable across cycles, and oriented toward implementation rather than consensus alone.
column13:
Global AI governance discussions remain dominated by tech hubs, policy elites, and English-speaking experts. This leaves rural populations, economically marginalized communities, and non-English linguistic groups largely unheard. Their absence shapes policies that often assume access, literacy, and infrastructure that these communities lack, embedding inequities in AI deployment and oversight.
Rural communities face structural exclusion: limited internet access, scarce digital literacy programs, and low representation in advisory bodies. Economically backward populations are further marginalized, as AI policy tends to prioritize commercial or urban use cases, ignoring local livelihoods, informal economies, or labor-intensive sectors vulnerable to automation. Linguistic diversity compounds this gap: most global fora operate in English, sidelining the perspectives of billions who navigate AI in regional languages or dialects.
Inclusion requires systemic adjustments. First, governance platforms must proactively engage local stakeholders through decentralized consultationsâ€”village councils, farmer cooperatives, and local NGOs can surface real-world risks and needs. Second, multilingual dissemination and participation must be standard: translation of policy drafts, AI literacy campaigns in local languages, and regional AI forums can amplify diverse voices. Third, economic accessibility should guide participation: stipends, travel support, and digital infrastructure can ensure communities with limited resources can engage meaningfully.
Finally, AI governance bodies should embed local representation structurally, not episodically. Reserved seats for rural, economically backward, and non-English linguistic communities in international advisory councils can shift policy design from top-down assumptions to grounded realities. Without this, AI governance risks entrenching inequity rather than addressing it.
In short, global AI discussions must move beyond urban, elite, English-speaking circles. Equity in AI policy emerges not from abstract principles but from listening to the communities most exposed to AIâ€™s uneven impacts.
column14:
I could see the below engagement formats for meaningful AI dialogue:

Equitable AI roundtables bring together stakeholders from underserved communities, rural regions, and non-English speaking populations. Small, facilitated groups ensure all voices are heard, highlighting issues of fairness, bias, and access that are often overlooked in global debates.

Policy simulations let with regulators, industry, and civil society actors navigating AI governance and digital public infrastructure (DPI) scenarios. These exercises reveal trade-offs, systemic gaps, and governance tensions, making abstract rules concrete and showing where interventions can be most effective.

Problem-focused panel discussions to connect AI to real infrastructure gaps. For example, AI for mental health in regions where care is scarce or taboo can be explored through co-design, scenario mapping, and culturally sensitive solution building. Similar workshops can address education, healthcare, and local governance, linking innovation to societal needs.
column15:
Effective AI governance emerges from policies and practices that combine accountability, inclusivity, and practical oversight. Top-down rules alone fail; solutions must engage communities, regulators, and industry simultaneously.
Risk-based regulatory frameworks define clear obligations linked to potential harm. The EU AI Act classifies systems by risk, setting legal standards for high-impact applications. Indiaâ€™s draft AI Policy emphasizes fairness, transparency, and alignment with local economic and social needs.
Standards and certification translate principles into measurable practices. ISO/IEC AI standards, for example, guide bias mitigation, data quality, and system robustness, making compliance verifiable.
Participatory platforms integrate marginalized voices into governance. Multi-stakeholder councils, citizen assemblies, and crowdsourced deliberation allow rural communities, non-English speakers, and economically disadvantaged groups to co-design AI rules and highlight ethical concerns.
Regulatory sandboxes provide controlled environments to pilot AI systems. Companies, regulators, and civil society test impacts before full deployment, reducing harm and informing policy adjustments.
Digital public infrastructure (DPI) approaches address gaps in access and equity. Open data, privacy-preserving sharing models, and interoperable standards allow AI to serve public needs example, AI-assisted mental health support in regions lacking professionals or facing cultural stigma.
Ethics and impact assessments embed accountability. Mandatory audits, algorithmic impact evaluations, and continuous monitoring convert governance from abstract principles into enforceable routines.
Together, these approaches create a layered governance ecosystem. AI oversight becomes actionable, inclusive, and responsive. It links innovation with societal outcomes, ensures safety, and prioritizes equity for communities often excluded from global policy discussions

column5:
Success would mean three concrete outcomes.
First, the Dialogue produces a shared recognition that AI governance is not solely a technical or regulatory matter it is also a cultural and narrative one. The stories AI systems generate, the voices they amplify or erase, and the values embedded in their outputs are governance questions of the first order. A successful Dialogue would explicitly name culture, artistic creation, and civil society creative practice as legitimate domains of governance discussion, not afterthoughts.
Second, the Dialogue establishes accountability mechanisms that are practice-based, not only compliance-based. Transparency frameworks for AI systems gain legitimacy when they emerge from the communities using those systems, including artists, educators, and civil society organisations  and are embedded in practice from inception rather than imposed retrospectively. A successful Dialogue would surface and validate such models, creating pathways for their wider adoption.
Third, the Dialogue advances a concrete agenda for bridging AI divides that goes beyond connectivity and compute. Cultural production who gets to create AI-generated content, in which language, anchored in which heritage is a dimension of AI equity that current frameworks systematically underaddress.
A successful Dialogue would commit to measuring and reducing this dimension of the divide.
For WE ARE HUMAN, a successful Dialogue would also be one that opens a durable channel between the UN system and civil society organisations working at the operational frontier of ethical AI practice, not only as observers, but as contributors to the ongoing governance architecture.
column6: Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;AI capacity-building;Protection and promotion of human rights;Transparency, accountability, and human oversight;
column7:
WE ARE HUMAN is a non-profit association and the convening body of the first international festival dedicated to AI-generated audiovisual works, grounded in an editorial framework aligned article by article with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Our four priorities reflect this positioning directly.
Cultural and societal implications are our primary lens. AI does not only automate tasks — it reshapes narratives, aesthetics, and collective memory. Governance frameworks must address this dimension explicitly, not absorb it into technical categories.
Human rights protection is our editorial architecture. Each of our 30 planned festival editions is anchored to one UDHR article. This structure demonstrates that the UDHR can serve as an operational compass for AI cultural production, not merely an aspirational reference.
Transparency and accountability are embedded in our practice through a mandatory instrument we call the Ethics Notebook: a public disclosure document accompanying each work, detailing the AI tools used, biases identified, data provenance, editorial choices made, and carbon footprint generated. This model shows that accountability works best when designed into practice from inception, not layered on as compliance.
Capacity-building matters to us because our inaugural edition deploys simultaneously across seven cities on four continents — including São Paulo, Johannesburg, and Taipei with a deliberate centering of the Global South. Bridging AI divides requires attending to cultural production capacity, not only computational infrastructure
column8:
Two significant gaps deserve the Dialogue's attention :
First: the governance of AI-generated culture as a distinct domain. Current frameworks treat cultural content primarily as a risk category  deepfakes, misinformation, copyright infringement. This framing is necessary but insufficient. It ignores the positive governance question: who gets to produce AI-generated culture, in whose language, drawing on whose heritage, under whose editorial authority? The concentration of AI cultural production in a small number of platforms and geographies is a governance problem as serious as the concentration of computational infrastructure  and it is not yet named as such in any major international framework.
Second: the relationship between AI governance and cultural diplomacy. AI-generated content is increasingly a vector of soft power shaping how nations, peoples, and histories are represented in global information flows. This intersection between AI governance and cultural diplomacy is absent from the current thematic clusters, yet it is operationally active: states and non-state actors are already using AI to project narratives internationally. A future iteration of the Dialogue should address the governance implications of AI as a diplomatic and geopolitical instrument, with particular attention to the perspectives of countries and communities whose cultural heritage is most at risk of misrepresentation or extraction.
WE ARE HUMAN's work directly addresses both gaps through its UDHR-anchored editorial architecture and its multi-continental deployment — and we would welcome the opportunity to contribute further to the Dialogue's reflection on these emerging dimensions.
column9:
The civil society and cultural sector faces a governance gap that is structural, not incidental. AI tools capable of generating images, voices, narratives, and audiovisual works at scale are now accessible to any organisation with minimal resources. Yet the frameworks governing their use in cultural production, in terms of transparency, rights, provenance, and accountability ,remain almost entirely absent at the international level.

For organisations working at the intersection of AI, human rights, and cultural diplomacy, this gap creates both acute challenges and genuine opportunities.

The central challenge is one of legitimacy. When civil society organisations use AI in cultural production — even deliberately, critically, and transparently — they operate without recognised standards or shared vocabulary. There is no international framework that validates ethical AI cultural practice, distinguishes it from extractive or manipulative uses, or provides the governance language needed to build trust with institutional partners, funders, and audiences. This absence weakens the credibility of responsible actors while offering no barrier to irresponsible ones.

A second challenge is geopolitical asymmetry. The cultural narratives produced and distributed through AI systems largely originate in a small number of technologically advanced countries. Communities in the Global South — whose oral traditions, heritage, and living cultures are among the richest in the world have limited capacity to shape how AI represents them, and limited recourse when it does so inaccurately or exploitatively. Governance frameworks that do not address this asymmetry will entrench it.

The opportunity, however, is real. Civil society organisations already developing practice-based accountability models such as embedded transparency instruments, multi-continental diffusion architectures, and editorial frameworks anchored in human rights  offer the Dialogue concrete, tested approaches that complement top-down regulatory frameworks with bottom-up governance practice.
column10:
The AI Dialogue's most distinctive potential contribution to international cooperation is one that no bilateral agreement, regional framework, or industry standard can replicate: it is the only universal forum where governments and civil society sit at the same table, with equal entitlement to shape the agenda.
That universality is not merely procedural it is substantive. AI governance challenges that are genuinely global in their consequences, but unequal in their distribution, require a forum where the countries and communities most affected by those consequences have standing. The Dialogue can be that forum, but only if it resists the tendency to treat governance as primarily a technical coordination problem among advanced economies.
For the cultural and civil society sector, the Dialogue's role in international cooperation is threefold.
First, it can establish shared vocabulary. One of the most significant obstacles to international cooperation on ethical AI in cultural production is the absence of common definitions for transparency, for accountability, for meaningful human oversight. The Dialogue can surface and validate terminology that travels across jurisdictions and sectors.
Second, it can create recognition pathways. Civil society organisations and cultural institutions working responsibly with AI lack any international mechanism to have that practice recognised, validated, or connected to others doing equivalent work in different contexts. The Dialogue can build those bridges.
Third, it can anchor norm formation in practice rather than aspiration. The most durable international norms emerge from documented practice, not declaration. By centering the experiences of practitioners  including artists, educators, and civil society organisations  alongside governments and industry, the Dialogue can generate governance insights grounded in what actually works.
column11:
Several existing frameworks and initiatives offer the AI Dialogue genuine foundations to build upon rather than duplicate.
UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI is the most directly relevant existing instrument for the cultural and civil society sector. It calls explicitly on member states to harness cultural and creative expression as vectors of ethical reflection on AI, and it provides a normative basis for the practice-based accountability models that civil society organisations are already developing. The Dialogue should treat the UNESCO Recommendation not as a reference document but as an operational framework to be advanced and monitored.
The Global Digital Compact, which mandated the Dialogue itself, established commitments on digital inclusion and the responsible use of emerging technologies that remain largely unimplemented in the cultural sector. The Dialogue should take stock of that implementation gap and identify civil society actors already working to close it.
At the practitioner level, initiatives that embed transparency and human rights accountability directly into AI creative processes — such as the Ethics Notebook framework developed within the WE ARE HUMAN festival — represent the kind of bottom-up governance practice that international frameworks rarely acknowledge but consistently need. Connecting these practices to the Dialogue's intergovernmental process would strengthen both.
Finally, the AI for Good Global Summit, in whose margins the first Dialogue session will be held, provides an immediate connection to the technical and innovation communities. The Dialogue's added value relative to that Summit is precisely its human rights and civil society dimension that differentiation should be preserved and strengthened, not blurred.
The Dialogue's unique contribution is not to replace existing mechanisms but to provide the universal, multi-stakeholder home they currently lack.
column12:
The AI Dialogue will only generate durable governance outcomes if it treats civil society not as an observer category but as a co-producer of knowledge. Governments bring regulatory authority. Industry brings technical capacity. Civil society brings something neither can replicate: direct accountability to the communities most affected by AI's consequences, and documented practice in navigating those consequences without institutional protection.

In practical terms, this means the Dialogue's format should reserve dedicated speaking time for civil society practitioners in each thematic session, not only in open floor segments where institutional voices naturally dominate. It also means that written inputs from civil society organisations should be synthesised and reflected in the Co-Chairs' summary, not treated as background documentation.

The two-day Geneva format is necessarily compressed. To make it generative rather than ceremonial, thematic breakout sessions should be structured around concrete case studies and documented practices, with practitioners presenting alongside government delegates. The goal of each session should be to surface at least one replicable model or actionable recommendation, not only to map the landscape of concerns.

Between sessions, the Dialogue should maintain a living repository of civil society contributions, openly accessible, which delegates and stakeholders can consult and build upon ahead of the 2027 New York session.
column13:
The most consequential underrepresentation in global AI governance discussions is not demographic  it is epistemological. The communities whose cultural heritage, oral traditions, and living knowledge systems are most exposed to AI's extractive logics are systematically absent from the rooms where governance norms are set.

Artists, storytellers, and cultural practitioners from the Global South hold deep expertise in exactly the questions AI governance must answer: whose knowledge counts, whose voice is authentic, whose heritage can be reproduced and by whom. That expertise is not recognised as governance knowledge in current frameworks.

Young people are similarly absent. They are the primary users of AI-generated content, the generation that will live longest with the governance decisions made now, and in many of the countries represented in Geneva, they constitute the majority of the population. Their perspectives should be structurally integrated, not invited as a gesture.

Finally, artists and cultural organisations working with AI in good faith occupy a distinctive position: they use these tools critically, transparently, and accountably, and they face the governance gaps directly in their daily practice. The WE ARE HUMAN festival is built on the conviction that this community has concrete contributions to make to governance, not only to aesthetics. The Dialogue should create pathways for that contribution.
column14:
The most effective formats for meaningful engagement are those that make governance stakes visible and tangible, not only discussable.

Opening each thematic session with a short work — a film, a testimony, a documented creative process — that concretely illustrates the governance challenge under discussion would shift the register from abstract policy to lived consequence. This is not decoration. It is a method for grounding intergovernmental exchange in the realities it is meant to address.

Structured peer exchange between practitioners from different regions, facilitated in small groups alongside the plenary sessions, would allow the kind of direct knowledge transfer that large-format meetings cannot produce. A civil society organisation running an AI ethics programme in Johannesburg and one doing equivalent work in Taipei have more to learn from each other than from another panel of experts — the Dialogue should create the conditions for that exchange.
column15:
The most instructive examples of effective AI governance are not found in regulatory texts — they are found in organisations that have made accountability operational, at the point of creation, with real works and real audiences.

WE ARE HUMAN is developing one such example directly. Our festival commissions AI-generated audiovisual works anchored to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and requires every work presented to be accompanied by an Ethics Notebook: a public document disclosing the AI tools used, the biases encountered and the choices made to navigate them, the cultural provenance of the data drawn upon, and the carbon cost of the generation process. This instrument has been tested in production with works addressing African oral heritage and post-colonial identity, created by artists from South Africa, for international presentation. It functions. It is replicable. It costs nothing to adopt beyond the editorial commitment to do so.

What this model demonstrates concretely is that human oversight does not require an external auditor or a regulatory body to be meaningful. It requires that the human beings making creative decisions document those decisions, expose them to public scrutiny, and treat transparency as a condition of legitimacy rather than a burden of compliance.

A second concrete practice worth the Dialogue's attention is multi-continental simultaneous diffusion as an equity instrument. Rather than exporting AI cultural content from technologically advanced countries to others, our festival architecture places cities in the Global South — Johannesburg, São Paulo, Taipei — as co-equal programme sites from the first edition. The governance insight here is simple: inclusion must be structural, not aspirational. It must be designed into the architecture of the initiative before the first work is shown, not added later as outreach.

These are not proposals. They are practices already underway, available to inform the Dialogue's recommendations.
Contact: Michael Swierczynski, President — mski@wearehuman.foundation / michaelswi06@gmail.com

column5:
A successful first Global Dialogue would achieve a clear international commitment to AI equity and move from principles to practice. It should outline relevant action areas and provide an actionable roadmap with concrete steps toward AI democratisation while addressing risks and aligning global rules for AI governance. Such a roadmap should recognise knowledge commons as foundational infrastructure for AI democratisation. This should be understood as not just access to AI technologies, but rather as enabling nations and communities to chart their own digital futures. This requires the ability to develop AI systems and solutions, adapt existing technologies to local contexts, and ensure agency in AI development and governance.
To this end, the Global Dialogue should reaffirm the Global Digital Compact's commitment to Digital Public Goods (DPGs), including open AI models, open data, and open-source software, and recognise that such goods are produced and maintained within knowledge commons: the communities, platforms, and shared infrastructures whose long-term sustainability is a necessary precondition for a digital future envisioned in the Compact. The Global Dialogue on AI urgently needs to recognize the role of the knowledge commons as critical infrastructure for AI that serves a people-centered digital world and humanity as a whole.
column6: Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;Protection and promotion of human rights;Transparency, accountability, and human oversight;Open-source software, open data and open AI models
column7:
Our perspective draws on Wikimedia CH's work at the intersection of knowledge commons, AI governance, and digital public infrastructure. We propose a thematic agenda centred on knowledge commons as a critical resource and infrastructure for AI. The four priorities address the foundations (open source, data and models), the implications of AI for the digital commons, the governance instruments required, and the normative anchoring of AI governance in international human rights.
The priority on open-source software, open data and open AI models recognises that knowledge commons, including collaboratively produced encyclopedic content, open datasets, and cultural heritage, constitute critical infrastructure for contemporary AI, comparable to compute and model architectures. The Global Dialogue needs to address their long-term sustainability and governance, building on commitments to Digital Public Goods and digital commons in the 2020 Roadmap for Digital Cooperation and the Global Digital Compact. A framing centred on knowledge commons as critical infrastructure for AI brings into focus the collaborative development and governance of open resources.
The priority on the social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI acknowledges the systemic transformations AI introduces in the production, distribution and access of knowledge. The focus should be on linguistic, epistemic and cultural plurality, which is a priority for Wikimedia CH in the context of Swiss values and the country's cultural and linguistic diversity. Protecting resilience and diversity is a matter of common concern.
The priority on transparency, accountability and robust human oversight reflects the need for governance instruments capable of translating these concerns into obligations. Reciprocity between AI and the knowledge commons, together with transparency, traceability and oversight, is necessary for public trust and responsible AI development. The priority on human rights anchors the agenda in international law: rights of access to information, freedom of expression, and participation in cultural life and scientific progress must be upheld in the development and deployment of AI.
column8:
We propose three cross-cutting issues that we consider central to global AI governance:
Knowledge commons: Knowledge commons are adjacent to, but distinct from, "open" resources (code, data or models). They include many other types of collaboratively produced, maintained and governed resources. In the context of AI development, sustainability of the knowledge commons is the key issue. Public support is needed, as well as measures that protect the commons from extraction of value, without giving back to the commons. Treating this as a cross-cutting concern allows the Dialogue to consider social, institutional and economic conditions under which open-source software, open data and open AI models are created.
Public AI: Public AI extends beyond open-source models to a broader, normative vision of AI grounded in public attributes (openness, interoperability), public functions (advancing public interest goals, including the Sustainable Development Goals), and public ownership or stewardship. Initiatives such as Apertus, the Swiss public multilingual large language model, demonstrate that publicly accountable AI development is feasible and complementary to commercial systems. Public AI and public interest AI development have been previously recognized in the Paris Charter on AI in the public interest.
Reciprocity: A norm of reciprocity between developers of AI systems and the communities and infrastructures on which they depend is currently absent from the multilateral debate. Reciprocity cuts across data governance, transparency, sustainability and human rights, and provides a single principle around which obligations toward Digital Public Goods, knowledge commons, and contributing communities can be articulated. Without such a norm, the long-term sustainability of the resources that AI relies upon cannot be secured. Reciprocity is also an important norm when considering global AI divide, and for ensuring democratization of AI capabilities in Global Majority contexts. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance needs to acknowledge the vital value of the knowledge commons as critical infrastructure for AI.
column9:
Wikimedia CH speaks from a Swiss perspective shaped by the European context and the global Wikimedia movement. Switzerland's tradition of neutrality, multilateral dialogue, and consensus-building, together with Geneva's positioning as a place of humanity and people-centered technology, make it a natural setting for governance that prioritises collaboration.
The most consequential governance gap across these environments is the absence of a coherent framework that recognises knowledge commons as critical infrastructure for AI and provides for their protection, sustainable funding, and democratic governance.
Two challenges stand out. First, knowledge commons such as Wikipedia and freely licensed cultural heritage are increasingly extracted as AI training inputs without reciprocity, oversight, or contribution to their long-term sustainability. The Wikimedia Foundation reports that AI crawlers now generate the majority of its highest-cost traffic. Second, public-interest alternatives remain limited, and Public AI is not yet recognised as a distinct policy vision in European or multilateral frameworks.
The opportunities lie in aligning multilateral commitments around policies that support not only open-source code and content, but also technical infrastructure, communities, and governance frameworks needed to sustain knowledge commons. Apertus, the Swiss multilingual large language model, shows that public institutions can build AI aligned with these commitments — and reflects Switzerland's capacity to translate its values into infrastructure. Financial mechanisms supporting the commons must also be explored; Wikimedia Enterprise illustrates one workable model of reciprocity with AI companies.
The Global Dialogue, hosted in Geneva, should connect national, regional, and multilateral processes around a shared recognition that digital commons are infrastructure warranting public investment and protection.
column10:
The AI Dialogue needs to facilitate discussions and collaborations between the different stakeholders working with and affected by AI. Wikimedia CH is an important stakeholder here, representing civil society while also being part of the Wikimedia movement, the Open-Source movement and integral to the knowledge commons.
The AI Dialogue needs to ensure that all voices are heard equally, and it needs to call for action against the widening of the global AI divide, but also against the immediate danger of shrinking epistemic diversity if AI does not reciprocate what it takes from the knowledge commons (see Question 12).
As transnational corporations become increasingly powerful and as they become more powerful than nation-states, formats such as the AI Dialogue have a special responsibility in amplifying the voices of those with little agency. The way AI is allowed to function now, it consumes the knowledge commons, the information humans have carefully introduced to the digital world, and gives nothing in return. If this human knowledge is not added to the digital anymore, the quality of information online will drastically degrade with harsh consequences for humanity worldwide.
In this context, collaboration across all sectors is needed now. Transnational corporations need to be held accountable when it comes to how AI consumes the knowledge commons, but there is also an increasing need for more awareness amongst policy makers globally regarding the prevention of these risks by means of appropriate regulations, and the value of knowledge commons and Digital Public Goods.
The AI Dialogue should play a crucial role here. By including the voices of Wikimedia CH and the Wikimedia Movement as a global collaboration platform, the Global Dialogue can ensure that the commitments of UN initiatives such as the Global Digital Compact gain wider recognition.
column11:
Initiatives the AI Dialogue should build upon are e.g. the 2020 Roadmap for Digital Cooperation, the Global Digital Compact, and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, all aimed at a more equitable digital world.
The WSIS+20 implementation in 2025 showed the global effort to build more people-centered, inclusive, and development-oriented digital societies, and offered additional guidance on AI. Technology is not neutral and it cannot exist without human interference. Wikimedia projects such as Wikipedia or Wikidata demonstrate how open, participatory projects can sustain knowledge infrastructure at global scale. This infrastructure is increasingly seen as a critical foundation for AI, but it should be more broadly considered as critical infrastructure that serves humanity.
The AI Dialogue taking place in Geneva points to certain Swiss values, such as humanity and people-centered tech, transparency and a culture of collaboration. The Dialogue can add value by moving toward coordinated global action, including integrating Digital Public Goods into national AI strategies, promoting interoperability, and supporting investment in shared infrastructure and standards required to support open source communities.
The AI Dialogue should connect the mentioned national, regional, and multilateral efforts around a shared understanding that digital commons are essential infrastructures that urgently need public investment and protection. For the AI Dialogue to provide greater coherence, interoperability, and mutual understanding across different stakeholders and processes, the key relation between the knowledge commons and AI must be addressed.
The AI Dialogue must also ensure that civil society perspectives are represented. In this context, the voices of the communities that preserve the Wikimedia projects need to be heard.
column12:
We suggest making a call for proposals to include civil society- and community-led sessions during the Global Dialogue. There is a critical need for more such perspectives on AI. Wikimedia CH would be pleased to co-chair panels or break-out sessions, e.g. together with other Wikimedia Affiliates, other organizations central to the knowledge commons or likeminded institutions and initiatives such as the Digital Public Goods Alliance.
This will help strengthen civil society perspectives and demonstrate the vital role the knowledge commons is playing for the information loop and especially for AI, all whilst not being sufficiently acknowledged and rewarded in return.
The impact AI is having on cultures and societies today must urgently get more attention in national and international debates and dialogues. Research perspectives from the intersections of social and cultural sciences as well as tech and AI are crucial here, and Wikimedia CH can make meaningful contributions in this regard.
column13:
Communities of the knowledge commons including the Wikimedia communities: Although they ensure the existence of the knowledge commons and therefore of epistemic resilience and diversity in the digital world, their perspectives are not sufficiently included in global discussion about AI governance. The people who contribute to these communities have to be empowered. Information is a fundamental human right, a human right that is threatened by the way AI is allowed to currently function. Stakeholders involved in AI governance need to give voice to communities that defend this right to information.
Projects such as Wikipedia or Wikidata, both officially recognized as Digital Public Goods (DPGs) by the UN-endorsed Digital Public Goods Alliance, must be at the center of AI governance discussions. At a time when a few international corporations increasingly dominate the digital world, ensuring that DPGs and the communities behind them are present in governance debates becomes a pressing necessity.
Global Majority voices, broadly speaking, also need to be included. The AI divide concerns people of the Global Majority specifically. Wikimedia CH is member of the WikiFranca initiative whose objective it is to connect the “francophonie” of Wikimedia, meaning French-speaking Wikimedia communities. This includes many communities of the African continent and it is an important endeavor for Wikimedia CH to represent these diverse communities and their perspectives on AI in a meaningful way.
column14:
We suggest a mix of interactive, multi-stakeholder, and action-oriented formats rather than long plenary-only sessions. The strongest options are ones that match the Dialogue’s inclusive, global, and fast-moving structure, especially given the emphasis on broad participation and practical outcomes. Concrete examples are small, mixed-stakeholder roundtables or lighting talks followed by structured Q&A.
Action-oriented plans are urgently needed in order to hold the corporations accountable that make AI consume the knowledge commons without reciprocating. The AI Dialogue is the place where such plans must be drafted.
column15:
The WSIS+20 implementation in 2025 showed the global effort to build a more people-centered, inclusive, and development-oriented digital society, and offered additional guidance on AI which Wikimedia CH supports. Another key initiative of the WSIS process is the national and international Internet Governance Forums, which have been providing a space for open dialogue on internet governance among civil society, the private sector, the technical community, governments and international organizations.
Apertus, the Swiss public multilingual large language model provides one more example. It demonstrates that publicly accountable AI development is feasible and complementary to commercial systems.
Another initiative is the DPG Standard of the Digital Public Goods Alliance. They promote AI governance by championing DPGs—open source software, data, and AI systems—as a foundational framework for transparency and equity. The DPG Standard is a primary tool in this effort, which includes specific criteria for AI systems as a category of Digital Public Goods.
Practices that offer concrete solutions have also been introduced in the context of the Wikimedia Movement. Wikimedia Enterprise, a service of the Wikimedia Foundation, shows that holding businesses accountable for reusing Wikimedia content at large scale by means of AI is possible. The need for more such initiatives has never been more critical.
Wikipedia’s community-led governance model itself demonstrates how transparency, human oversight, and participatory decision-making can operate effectively at global scale, while its verifiability and reliable sourcing standards help sustain a high-quality information ecosystem that is critical for AI systems relying on large-scale data.
All these initiatives address key problematics of AI and call for a more equitable, sustainable digital society that takes into account linguistic and cultural plurality. The consumption of the knowledge commons by AI is however an issue that remains highly underrepresented.

column5:
Un primer Diálogo Mundial sobre Gobernanza de la IA sería exitoso si logra pasar de declaraciones generales a compromisos concretos que reflejen la diversidad del mundo y reduzcan las brechas existentes en el ecosistema digital.
Desde la perspectiva de Wikimedia Colombia, esto implica que las voces de comunidades históricamente subrepresentadas —incluyendo pueblos indígenas, comunidades rurales, comunidades campesinas y grupos lingüísticos diversos— no solo estén presentes, sino que incidan de manera efectiva en las decisiones. El éxito se vería en la adopción de mecanismos claros para garantizar su participación continua, informada y vinculante en la gobernanza de la IA.
Asimismo, sería clave avanzar en acuerdos que promuevan la equidad en el acceso al conocimiento y a las tecnologías de IA. Esto incluye compromisos para desarrollar sistemas que respeten y fortalezcan la diversidad lingüística y cultural, evitando la homogenización de contenidos y la reproducción de sesgos que invisibilizan saberes locales. Otro resultado fundamental sería el reconocimiento del conocimiento como un bien común, impulsando políticas que favorezcan modelos abiertos, colaborativos y transparentes. En este sentido, la articulación con movimientos como Wikimedia puede aportar experiencias concretas sobre gobernanza participativa y producción colectiva de conocimiento.
Finalmente, el diálogo será exitoso si establece una hoja de ruta clara con mecanismos de seguimiento, rendición de cuentas y cooperación internacional, especialmente entre el Norte y el Sur Global. Sin estos elementos, el riesgo es que el proceso quede en lo declarativo.
Es decir, el éxito radica en construir una gobernanza de la IA más inclusiva, justa y representativa, donde la diversidad no sea un principio abstracto, sino una práctica efectiva.
column6: Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;Protection and promotion of human rights;Open-source software, open data and open AI models;AI capacity-building
column7:
Nuestra selección responde a la necesidad de promover una gobernanza de la IA centrada en la equidad, la diversidad y el conocimiento como bien común.
En primer lugar, las implicaciones sociales, culturales y lingüísticas de la IA son una prioridad porque los sistemas actuales tienden a reproducir sesgos y a invisibilizar conocimientos locales. Para Wikimedia Colombia, es fundamental que la IA reconozca y fortalezca la diversidad cultural y lingüística, especialmente de comunidades indígenas y subrepresentadas.
En segundo lugar, la protección y promoción de los derechos humanos es esencial para garantizar que el desarrollo y uso de la IA no profundice desigualdades existentes. Esto incluye salvaguardar derechos como el acceso al conocimiento, la participación y la no discriminación en entornos digitales.
El desarrollo de capacidades en IA es otra prioridad clave, ya que cerrar brechas digitales implica no solo acceso a tecnología, sino también la posibilidad de comprenderla, adaptarla y participar en su gobernanza. Fortalecer capacidades en comunidades diversas permite una participación más equitativa y significativa.
Finalmente, el software de código abierto, datos abiertos y modelos de IA abiertos se alinean con nuestra visión de conocimiento libre y colaborativo. Estos enfoques fomentan la transparencia, la innovación inclusiva y la posibilidad de que más actores contribuyan a la construcción de tecnologías que respondan a contextos locales. En conjunto, estas prioridades buscan una IA más inclusiva, participativa y representativa de la diversidad global.
column8:
Sí. Si bien las áreas identificadas cubren aspectos fundamentales, existen cuestiones transversales y emergentes que merecen mayor atención.
Una de ellas es la justicia epistémica y la representación del conocimiento. La IA no solo procesa datos, sino que define qué conocimientos son visibles, legítimos o útiles. Esto plantea el riesgo de profundizar la exclusión de saberes indígenas, locales y no occidentales si no se incorporan activamente en los sistemas de datos y modelos.
Otra cuestión clave es la soberanía de datos y gobernanza comunitaria. Más allá del acceso abierto, es necesario reconocer el derecho de las comunidades —especialmente indígenas— a decidir sobre la recopilación, uso y circulación de sus datos y conocimientos, respetando principios como el consentimiento libre, previo e informado.
También es relevante la sostenibilidad social y ambiental de la IA. El desarrollo de estas tecnologías tiene impactos materiales (consumo energético, uso de recursos) y sociales (condiciones laborales en la cadena de datos) que suelen quedar fuera del debate de gobernanza.
Finalmente, la inclusión significativa en la producción tecnológica sigue siendo un desafío transversal. No basta con consultar a comunidades diversas; es necesario crear condiciones para su participación activa en el diseño, desarrollo y evaluación de sistemas de IA.
Estas cuestiones complementan los temas existentes y son esenciales para avanzar hacia una gobernanza de la IA verdaderamente inclusiva y contextualizada.
column9:
En Colombia y en la región latinoamericana, las brechas en la gobernanza de la IA se manifiestan principalmente en la desigualdad en el acceso, la representación y la capacidad de incidencia en el desarrollo tecnológico.
Uno de los principales retos es la subrepresentación de contextos locales, lenguas y saberes en los datos que alimentan los sistemas de IA. Esto limita la pertinencia de estas tecnologías y puede reforzar sesgos que afectan a comunidades indígenas, rurales y otras poblaciones históricamente excluidas. A esto se suma una brecha significativa en el desarrollo de capacidades, que dificulta la participación activa de estos grupos en la creación y gobernanza de la IA. Asimismo, persisten desafíos en la protección de derechos humanos, particularmente en relación con la privacidad, el uso de datos y la no discriminación. La falta de marcos robustos y contextualizados puede derivar en usos de la IA que amplíen desigualdades existentes.
Sin embargo, también existen oportunidades relevantes. El creciente interés regional por avanzar en políticas de IA abre espacios para incorporar enfoques inclusivos y participativos desde etapas tempranas. Iniciativas basadas en tecnologías abiertas y conocimiento libre permiten fortalecer ecosistemas colaborativos y adaptados a contextos locales. Además, el trabajo con comunidades diversas, como el que impulsa Wikimedia Colombia, demuestra que es posible co-crear contenidos, datos y capacidades de manera participativa, sentando bases para una gobernanza más equitativa.
En este contexto, cerrar las brechas no solo implica regular mejor la IA, sino también fortalecer la inclusión, la colaboración y el reconocimiento de la diversidad como elementos centrales del desarrollo tecnológico.
column10:
El Diálogo sobre IA puede desempeñar un papel clave como espacio de articulación para construir una gobernanza global más inclusiva, equilibrada y cooperativa. En primer lugar, puede facilitar la participación significativa de actores diversos, especialmente del Sur Global, comunidades locales y grupos históricamente subrepresentados. Esto contribuiría a equilibrar las asimetrías actuales en la toma de decisiones y a asegurar que las políticas reflejen una mayor pluralidad de contextos y realidades.
Asimismo, el Diálogo puede impulsar la convergencia de principios y marcos normativos, promoviendo estándares compartidos en torno a derechos humanos, transparencia y equidad. Esta interoperabilidad es fundamental para evitar fragmentaciones que dificulten la cooperación internacional. Otro aporte clave es el fomento de alianzas multiactor y redes de colaboración, que integren gobiernos, sociedad civil, academia y sector tecnológico. En este sentido, el intercambio de buenas prácticas —como modelos de conocimiento abierto y gobernanza participativa— puede fortalecer capacidades y acelerar aprendizajes colectivos.El Diálogo también puede movilizar compromisos para el desarrollo de capacidades en países y comunidades con menos recursos, reduciendo brechas y promoviendo una participación más equitativa en el ecosistema global de IA.
Finalmente, su valor dependerá de su capacidad para traducirse en mecanismos concretos de seguimiento, financiamiento y rendición de cuentas, que sostengan la cooperación más allá del evento. De esta manera, el Diálogo puede actuar como catalizador de una cooperación internacional más justa, donde la diversidad y el conocimiento compartido sean pilares de la gobernanza de la IA.
column11:
El Diálogo sobre IA debería apoyarse en iniciativas y marcos ya existentes para evitar duplicidades y potenciar aprendizajes acumulados. Entre ellos, destacan los Principios de IA de la UNESCO y su enfoque en derechos humanos, diversidad cultural y ética; los procesos de la OCDE y el G20 sobre políticas de IA; así como espacios multiactor como el Foro de Gobernanza de Internet (IGF), que han demostrado la importancia de la participación diversa. También es clave articularse con iniciativas regionales en América Latina que promueven políticas de IA con enfoque inclusivo, así como con redes de sociedad civil y movimientos de conocimiento abierto como Wikimedia, que aportan тәжіencias en gobernanza participativa y producción colaborativa.
Asimismo, deberían considerarse marcos emergentes sobre datos y gobernanza comunitaria, especialmente aquellos impulsados por pueblos indígenas y comunidades locales, que ofrecen perspectivas críticas sobre soberanía de datos y consentimiento. El valor añadido del Diálogo sobre IA radica en su capacidad de conectar estos esfuerzos en un espacio verdaderamente global, elevando voces que suelen quedar fuera de otros foros y promoviendo una mayor coherencia entre iniciativas. Puede actuar como puente entre niveles local, regional y global, facilitando la traducción de principios en acciones concretas.
Además, puede fortalecer la coordinación entre actores y promover compromisos vinculantes, mecanismos de seguimiento y financiamiento para implementar lo acordado. En este sentido, su aporte no sería crear nuevos marcos, sino integrar, amplificar y operacionalizar los existentes desde una perspectiva más inclusiva y equitativa.
column12:
Las distintas partes implicadas pueden contribuir al Diálogo sobre IA desde sus capacidades y responsabilidades diferenciadas, siempre bajo un enfoque multiactor y colaborativo.
Los gobiernos pueden aportar marcos normativos, compromisos de política pública y mecanismos de implementación. El sector privado puede contribuir con transparencia en el desarrollo de tecnologías, apertura de datos y modelos, y adopción de estándares éticos. La sociedad civil —incluyendo organizaciones como Wikimedia— puede garantizar la representación de intereses públicos, promover la inclusión y aportar тәжіencias en gobernanza participativa. La academia puede ofrecer evidencia, investigación crítica y evaluación de impactos. Por su parte, las comunidades locales e indígenas deben ser reconocidas como actores clave, no solo como beneficiarias, aportando conocimientos situados y perspectivas esenciales para una IA contextualizada.
En cuanto al formato, el Diálogo debería estructurarse de manera participativa, descentralizada e inclusiva. Se recomienda combinar espacios globales con consultas regionales y locales previas, que permitan recoger insumos diversos. Es clave garantizar condiciones de participación efectiva (idioma, accesibilidad, recursos). Asimismo, el proceso debería incluir mesas temáticas multiactor, mecanismos claros para integrar aportes en resultados concretos y espacios de co-creación, no solo de discusión.
Finalmente, es fundamental que el Diálogo incorpore una estructura de seguimiento, con metas, indicadores y rendición de cuentas, así como mecanismos de financiamiento para implementar lo acordado. Más que un evento aislado, el Diálogo debe concebirse como un proceso continuo que fortalezca la cooperación y la inclusión en la gobernanza global de la IA.
column13:
En los debates globales sobre gobernanza de la IA persiste una subrepresentación significativa de comunidades del Sur Global, especialmente pueblos indígenas, comunidades rurales, hablantes de lenguas minorizadas, mujeres, juventudes y organizaciones de base comunitaria. También están poco presentes quienes contribuyen a la producción de conocimiento abierto y quienes experimentan de manera directa los impactos de la IA sin participar en su diseño. Esta exclusión no es solo geográfica, sino también epistémica y lingüística: muchos espacios privilegian perspectivas técnicas y anglófonas, dejando por fuera formas diversas de conocimiento, como saberes ancestrales y comunitarios.
Para revertir esta situación, es necesario pasar de la inclusión simbólica a una participación significativa y vinculante. Esto implica diseñar procesos desde el inicio con estas comunidades, garantizando condiciones habilitantes como acceso a información clara, recursos para participar, traducción e interpretación en múltiples lenguas y formatos accesibles. Asimismo, se deben fortalecer mecanismos de consulta y co-creación a nivel local y regional, cuyos resultados incidan directamente en los espacios globales. El reconocimiento de enfoques como la gobernanza comunitaria de datos y el consentimiento libre, previo e informado es clave, especialmente en el trabajo con pueblos indígenas.
También es fundamental apoyar el desarrollo de capacidades para que más actores puedan participar en igualdad de condiciones, no solo como consultados, sino como co-diseñadores de políticas y tecnologías. Iniciativas basadas en el conocimiento abierto y colaborativo, como el movimiento Wikimedia, ofrecen modelos concretos para ampliar la participación y construir una gobernanza más representativa.
column14:
Para fomentar un compromiso significativo y dinámico, el Diálogo sobre IA debería ir más allá de los formatos tradicionales y adoptar metodologías participativas, inclusivas y adaptadas a contextos diversos. Un formato clave son los procesos deliberativos multiactor, como asambleas ciudadanas o jurados de ciudadanos, que permitan a personas de distintos contextos comprender, debatir y formular recomendaciones informadas sobre IA. Estos espacios fortalecen la legitimidad y diversidad de perspectivas.
Asimismo, los laboratorios de co-creación (co-creation labs) pueden facilitar el trabajo conjunto entre comunidades, gobiernos, academia y sector tecnológico para diseñar soluciones concretas, prototipos o lineamientos de política pública. Los diálogos descentralizados y regionales son fundamentales para recoger insumos desde contextos locales. Estos pueden combinarse con plataformas digitales abiertas donde se documenten y sistematicen aportes, asegurando transparencia y trazabilidad. También es valioso incorporar formatos interculturales, como diálogos basados en narrativas, metodologías comunitarias o encuentros facilitados por líderes locales, que reconozcan otras formas de producir y compartir conocimiento más allá de lo técnico.
El uso de plataformas colaborativas abiertas (por ejemplo, tipo wiki) permitiría la construcción colectiva y continua de documentos, recomendaciones y marcos de gobernanza, alineándose con principios de conocimiento libre.Finalmente, se pueden integrar mecanismos de retroalimentación continua, como consultas públicas iterativas y espacios de seguimiento participativo, que mantengan el compromiso más allá del evento. Estos formatos, combinados, pueden contribuir a una participación más inclusiva, horizontal y orientada a resultados concretos.
column15:
Existen diversas iniciativas que ofrecen aprendizajes valiosos para una gobernanza eficaz de la IA, especialmente desde enfoques inclusivos y basados en derechos. A nivel normativo, la Recomendación sobre la Ética de la IA de la UNESCO destaca por su enfoque centrado en derechos humanos, diversidad cultural y equidad, incluyendo lineamientos sobre impacto social, gobernanza de datos y sostenibilidad.
En el ámbito de prácticas, los principios CARE (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) para la gobernanza de datos indígenas constituyen un referente clave para garantizar el respeto a la soberanía de datos y el consentimiento de comunidades, complementando marcos más técnicos como los principios FAIR. Desde el enfoque de conocimiento abierto, plataformas como Wikimedia demuestran cómo la colaboración distribuida, la transparencia y la gobernanza participativa pueden sostener ecosistemas globales de información. Estas prácticas son relevantes para el desarrollo de datasets y modelos de IA más diversos y auditables.
En términos de política pública, algunas estrategias nacionales de IA en América Latina han comenzado a incorporar enfoques de inclusión y ética, promoviendo el desarrollo de capacidades y la participación multiactor, aunque aún enfrentan retos en su implementación. Asimismo, herramientas como las evaluaciones de impacto algorítmico (Algorithmic Impact Assessments) ofrecen mecanismos concretos para anticipar riesgos, mejorar la rendición de cuentas y fortalecer la supervisión humana en sistemas de IA.
Finalmente, los espacios multiactor como el Foro de Gobernanza de Internet (IGF) aportan metodologías de diálogo abierto e inclusivo que pueden inspirar procesos más participativos en la gobernanza de la IA. En conjunto, estos ejemplos muestran que una gobernanza eficaz requiere articular marcos éticos, herramientas prácticas y modelos participativos.

column5:
The first Global Dialogue will be successful if it can reinforce the commitment to the common principles of the Global Digital Compact and the sustainable development goals as a starting point that will be guarding its discussions, its outcomes and planning in the future. They should be guided by a philosophy of sharing, openness, and collaboration, central to earlier internet governance processes such as the vision of WSIS, and adopt it to AI governance. As structural imbalances are already emerging, adopting a holistic and risk-based approach that considers technical, social, cultural, economic and human-rights impact needs a prominent slot on the discussion schedule.
Furthermore, a successful first Global Dialogue should move from principles to implementation by securing global commitment to equitable, democratic, and multistakeholder AI governance. It should deliver an actionable roadmap that aligns global approaches, reduces fragmentation across governance processes such as WSIS+20 and the Global Digital Compact, and translates shared principles into concrete commitments by all stakeholders.
For Wikimedia Deutschland e.V., the Global Digital Compact’s commitment to digital public goods (DPGs)—including open knowledge, open data, and open-source software - are foundational building blocks for a more inclusive AI ecosystem that is multilingual and human-rights respecting. As AI systems increasingly rely on openly available, human-created knowledge, there is growing asymmetry between extraction and contribution, with large-scale reuse placing strain on public-interest digital infrastructure while reducing visibility and participation. Sustainable AI governance must therefore include norms for responsible reuse, attribution, and support for the digital commons. These norms need to include protection and support for the contributing communities. Equitable access to generative and symbolic AI technologies requires enabling communities to shape their own digital futures, develop local solutions, and participate meaningfully in governance processes.
column6: Social, economic, ethical, cultural, linguistic and technical implications of AI;Interoperability of governance approaches;Transparency, accountability, and human oversight;Open-source software, open data and open AI models
column7:
Knowledge is power and AI is transforming what knowledge is presented, how and by whom knowledge is produced, distributed, and accessed. This results in social and economic, but also ethical, cultural and linguistic implications. Use of generative AI solutions need to pass qualifiers for adequacy for example. Governance must address the risks of reinforcing existing inequities and ensure that it supports knowledge equity and everyone’s ability to participate in the creation of shared knowledge.
Interoperability of governance approaches because AI governance is developing across multiple processes. Without coordination, we risk fragmentation and duplication, less impact and effectiveness. Interoperability of governance approaches such as the WSIS process and the Global Digital Compact can create coherence, shared standards and mutual learning across frameworks. This is especially important for protecting digital commons and communities that are supporting them, as they are global by nature and require aligned policies across jurisdictions.
Transparency, accountability, and human oversight are critical for a functioning system in general and they are critical to maintaining trustworthy and verifiable information ecosystems. The ability to monitor, debate, and revise knowledge, with community-developed policies that govern shared online spaces, is essential to safeguard information integrity and ensure that AI systems remain adequately representative of and aligned with societal values.
Free and open-source software and open data are core components required to cultivate a culture of sharing and developing, that enable robust digital commons like Wikipedia or civic tech projects like Decidim or OpenStreetMap. Only when content can be legally shared, edited, and reused, online collaboration and creation can flourish. That openness must be paired with responsible governance by the affected communities. Public investment and governance are needed to protect these shared resources and the communities that maintain them. Protection and promotion of human rights are an essential part of that protection.
column8: Power accumulation is affecting the internet as such. Existing AI solutions are entrenching existing concentrations of power not the least due to political and economic alignment. The companies that provide major global AI solutions control nearly every layer of the value chain — from subsea cables and data centers to cloud services and chip supply. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance needs to address that AI technologies result in changes that could transform access and use of the internet as we know it, as the control over that infrastructure belongs to a few companies and the states that support them. We see already that adherence to rules and regulations is not always easy for powerful players, while the reinforcement of a rules based system would benefit all, no matter if technology or policy are concerned.
column9:
From a German and European perspective, the most significant governance gap is the absence of a coherent, unifying philosophy of how a global digital infrastructure that is affecting global power structures of the future should look like. We should remember the foundations and the successes of European unification as well as earlier internet governance processes such as WSIS: they relied on a philosophy of sharing, openness and collaboration. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance needs to manifest that collaboration rather than exclusion will be beneficial for all.
Consequently, the Global Dialogue on AI Governance should focus on Digital Public Goods as global examples of cooperation, openness and shared infrastructure, not only with mechanics and content, but also in self-governance. The Global Dialogue should help establish shared recognition that digital commons are infrastructure deserving attention, care, public investment and protection.
column10:
The AI Dialogue should function as a bridge. It can combine governance processes with global knowledge and experiences and come up with practical solutions and even decisions while helping prevent fragmentation. Strong coordination with existing multistakeholder platforms such as the Internet Governance Forum will not only energize these institutions through strengthened knowledge coherence and mutual learning but also add meaning through recommendations as a result of these discussion processes.
The Dialogue must address the widening global AI divide and amplify civil-society voices. Without reciprocity and safeguards, AI risks undermining epistemic diversity and the sustainability of knowledge ecosystems. By connecting stakeholders and reinforcing commitments from UN initiatives, the Dialogue can help translate shared principles into coordinated global action.
column11:
The Dialogue should build on existing frameworks including the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Digital Compact, the WSIS process or the Hamburg Declaration on Sustainable AI.
It should also connect with the Sustainable Development Goals as we can see a much needed and necessary link to the environmental consequences of AI solutions. Similarly, the impacts on free trade, equal access to markets, and fair competition need to be addressed at relevant global initiatives and representatives of these need to be invited to the Dialogue.
Existing digital governance multistakeholder processes such as the Internet Governance Forum need to be a sounding board for the Global Dialogue on AI and ideally the times and meeting locations should be merged, to ease the burden for participation.
The added value of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance lies in creating coherence across initiatives and establishing a shared understanding that openness, sharing, and collaboration are central to AI Governance as well as to Internet Governance in general.
column12:
The Global Dialogue should feature multistakeholder representation at all levels. As a consequence, the Dialogue should not only include civil-society and community-led sessions through open calls for proposals, but also co-chaired and multistakeholder sessions. Organisations such as Wikimedia Deutschland can contribute expertise at the intersection of AI, knowledge commons and digital public infrastructure.
Interdisciplinary participation — especially from social sciences and humanities — is essential to reflect AI’s societal and cultural impacts.
column13:
Key underrepresented groups include Global Majority voices in general. More specifically representatives from the AI value chain like click-workers, assembly-line workers, minority languages, knowledge-commons communities, including Wikimedia contributors, Open-source and Digital Public Goods developers, health and environment specialists have to be included.
Participation should be supported by adhering to the NETmundial+10 Sao Paulo Principles and include easy access to knowledge, timely notification of events, travel funding, multilingual formats or rules that reinforce multistakeholder representation within each track.
column14:
The Dialogue should prioritise interactive and action-oriented formats, including small multistakeholder roundtables, lightning talks with structured discussions, and working groups tasked with producing concrete commitments. Such formats are essential to move from dialogue to implementation, and to develop practical approaches to reciprocity and sustainability.
In addition, we propose intentionally framing the shared experience with informal moments: an optional group meditation about 15 minutes before the first session to support focus and presence, and a closing group hike to encourage informal networking, trust-building, and lasting collaboration.
column15:
Key examples include: Global Digital Compact, WSIS+20 Resolution, UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Internet Governance Forum (especially intersessional work such as the Policy Network on AI)
Wikimedia’s projects offer concrete, field-tested approaches to AI governance grounded in openness, human rights, and public-interest infrastructure. Wikipedia’s community-led governance model demonstrates how transparency, human oversight, and participatory decision-making can operate effectively at global scale, while its verifiability and reliable sourcing standards help sustain a high-quality information ecosystem that is critical for AI systems relying on large-scale data. Wikimedia’s use of open licensing, combined with structured access pathways such as APIs and services like Wikimedia Enterprise, illustrates how openness can be paired with responsible and sustainable reuse models, including attribution and contribution back. More broadly, Wikimedia projects function as knowledge infrastructure and digital public goods, underscoring the need to support shared resources that underpin trustworthy and inclusive AI. These approaches align with and complement broader multistakeholder efforts including participation at convenings like the Internet Governance Forum and the Wikimedia Foundation's membership in the Freedom Online Coalition and the Digital Public Goods Alliance, both of which promote human rights-based, transparent, and accountable digital governance frameworks.
Together, these initiatives demonstrate pathways toward a transparent, equitable and sustainable AI ecosystem grounded in the protection of digital commons.

column2: WINAR Institute for AI Policy and Governance in Africa
column5:
Success is not another framework document. Success is when the outcomes of this Dialogue are actually implementable by a government regulatory body that was formed eighteen months ago, or a hospital in rural Kenya that has no compliance team.
That means three concrete things.
First, a shared accountability standard for high-risk AI deployments not principles, but a documented minimum: who authorized the system, under what conditions, who is liable when harm occurs. Simple, enforceable, universally applicable.
Second, governance tools designed for low-resource institutional environments. Audit toolkits. Assessment templates. Practical instruments that organizations without legal teams can actually use. If the only people who can implement the outcomes of this Dialogue are already-resourced institutions in high-income countries, this Dialogue has failed.
Third, a mechanism that gives developing country governments real power to interrogate AI systems deployed by international vendors within their borders. Not a recommendation. A mechanism.
Success looks like Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra being able to use what comes out of Geneva. That is the test.
